The `NOT INDEXED` variant of each type stores the value but excludes it from the search index. This reduces storage and indexing overhead for fields that only need to be returned in results, not queried.

---

## JSON Type

The `JSON` type stores an entire JSON object as a single field. All leaf values within the object — regardless of nesting depth — are indexed and queryable as strings. This approach avoids requiring a fixed schema for nested data, making it well-suited for semi-structured or dynamic payloads.

**Key behaviors:**

- **Leaf values are indexed by dot-path.** A field defined as `metadata JSON` indexes every leaf value under its dot-path — e.g. `metadata.version`, `metadata.source.region` — as an exact-match string.
- **All comparisons are string-based.** Even numeric or date values stored inside a JSON field are compared as strings. Use `TEXT`, `INTEGER`, `DOUBLE`, etc. for fields that require numeric or range queries.
- **Dynamic nesting is supported.** The sub-field structure does not need to be declared in the schema — any JSON shape can be stored and its leaf values will be indexed automatically.

**Example:**

```sql
CREATE TABLE events (
    id      UUID,
    ts      DATE,
    payload JSON
) ;
```

A record with `payload = {"source": {"region": "us-east"}, "retries": 3}` indexes the leaf values `payload.source.region` and `payload.retries`. Note that `retries` is indexed as the string `'3'`, not the number `3`.

Migration `WHERE` clauses accept only simple column names, so dot-path filtering is not available in `UPDATE`/`DELETE` statements.

For `JSON NOT INDEXED`, the object is stored and returned in query results but none of its sub-fields can be queried.

---

## Composite Types

OBJECT, NESTED, and UNION allow structured sub-documents to be defined inline. All composite types enforce `dynamic: strict` on their sub-fields — new sub-fields must be added via `ALTER TABLE`, not inserted ad-hoc.

Composite types are recursive: OBJECT inside NESTED, NESTED inside OBJECT, and other combinations are all valid.

### OBJECT

Defines an embedded object with declared sub-fields. The column holds one object or a list of them: Elasticsearch indexes a list by flattening each sub-field into an array (`tags.label: ['a', 'b']`, `tags.value: [...]`), so a query on any one sub-field matches across the whole list, and the document returns the list as stored. This is the column type for every list of objects unless the query described under [NESTED](#nested) applies.

**Syntax:**

```sql
<column_name> OBJECT (<sub_column> <type> [, <sub_column> <type>]*) [NOT INDEXED]
```

- `NOT INDEXED` (optional): disables the object. The data is stored but cannot be searched or accessed via field paths.

**Example:**

```sql
CREATE TABLE persons (
    id KEYWORD,
    address OBJECT (street TEXT, city KEYWORD, state KEYWORD, zip KEYWORD)
);

-- Store but do not index the payload object
CREATE TABLE events (
    id KEYWORD,
    payload OBJECT (raw TEXT, size INTEGER) NOT INDEXED
);
```

### NESTED

Defines a list of embedded objects where each element is indexed as its own hidden document. Use it only when a query must match two sub-fields of the **same element** — `tags.label = 'env' AND tags.value = 'prod'` as one tag, not one tag's label and another tag's value — which the flattening an `OBJECT` column performs cannot express. Every element is a separate Lucene document, reached with a `nested` query and `inner_hits`, counted against `index.mapping.nested_objects.limit`, and rewritten whenever the parent document is updated, so a list that is read whole or queried by one sub-field is an `OBJECT` column. See the Elasticsearch reference on the [nested field type](https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/elasticsearch/mapping-reference/nested).

**Syntax:**

```sql
<column_name> NESTED (<sub_column> <type> [, <sub_column> <type>]*)
```

NESTED does not support `NOT INDEXED`.

**Example:**

```sql
CREATE TABLE articles (
    id KEYWORD,
    tags NESTED (label TEXT, value KEYWORD)
);
```

### UNION

Defines a field that can hold one of several named object variants. All variant fields are merged into a single flat object. Fields that appear in multiple variants must have the same type.

**Syntax:**

```sql
<column_name> UNION (
    <VariantName> (<sub_column> <type> [, <sub_column> <type>]*) [, ...]
) [NOT INDEXED]
```

- `NOT INDEXED` (optional): disables the merged object.
- Include a shared discriminator field (e.g. `kind KEYWORD`) in each variant so application code can identify which variant it received.

**Example:**

```sql
CREATE TABLE assets (
    id KEYWORD,
    item UNION (
        Book  (kind KEYWORD, title TEXT, isbn KEYWORD),
        Video (kind KEYWORD, title TEXT, duration INTEGER)
    )
);
```

The resulting `item` field is a single object with properties `kind`, `title`, `isbn`, and `duration`.

<callout type="warning">

**Limitation: shared OBJECT/NESTED/UNION fields across variants.** If two variants declare a field with the same name and the same composite type (OBJECT, NESTED, or UNION), only the first variant's sub-field definitions are used. The second variant's sub-fields are silently dropped. Conflict detection only applies to scalar types — it will not throw if two same-named OBJECT fields have different sub-structures.

To avoid this, ensure that any field shared across variants with a composite type has identical sub-fields in every variant. Scalar shared fields (such as a `kind KEYWORD` discriminator) are always safe.

</callout>

---

## Expressions

Expressions appear on the right of an `UPDATE ... SET` assignment.

- **Values:** any form in [Values](#values) — `'string'`, `123`, `12.5`, `-3`, `true`, `false`, `{ ... }`, `[ ... ]`
- **Parameters:** `:name`
- **Binary Expressions:** `<field> + <value>`, `<field> - <value>`, `<field> * <value>`, `<field> / <value>`; a comparison belongs in the `WHERE` clause

A binary expression reads the named field from the stored document, so its operands are scalars; object and array literals are only meaningful as a whole value.

---

## Keywords

Keywords match in any case: `SELECT`, `select` and `Select` are the same keyword. The literals `true`, `false` and `null` match in any case too, and cannot be used as a name, though an object literal can carry such a field name as a quoted key (`{ 'null': 1 }`).

Only the words that structure a statement are reserved:

`ALTER`, `AND`, `AS`, `BY`, `CREATE`, `DELETE`, `FROM`, `GROUP`, `INSERT`, `INTO`, `LIMIT`, `NOT`, `OR`, `ORDER`, `REINDEX`, `SELECT`, `SET`, `UPDATE`, `VALUES`, `WHERE`, `WITH`

Every other keyword, such as a type (`date`, `text`, `keyword`) or an option (`size`, `query`, `script`), is also a name wherever a name can appear, so a field can be called `date` or `size`. A reserved word is a name when double-quoted: `SELECT "order" FROM Order`.

### Case

Keywords ignore case. Names do not: an entity, field or alias name is written exactly the way the entity class spells it, since that is how it is stored. `firstName`, `FirstName` and `FIRSTNAME` are three different fields.

A name in the wrong case behaves differently depending on what it names:

- **An entity name** in the wrong case fails the statement, and the error names the entity you meant: `Application shop has no published entity named person; did you mean Person?`
- **A field name** in the wrong case is not an error. It names a field no row has, so **you get nothing**: a `SELECT` or aggregate returns no rows, and an `UPDATE` or `DELETE` changes none. When a query unexpectedly returns nothing, check the case of its field names first.

```sql
-- the same statement: keywords in any case
SELECT COUNT(*) AS total FROM Person WHERE lastName = 'Doe';
select count(*) as total from Person where lastName = 'Doe';

-- fails: no entity is named person
SELECT COUNT(*) AS total FROM person WHERE lastName = 'Doe';

-- returns nothing: LASTNAME is not the lastName field
SELECT COUNT(*) AS total FROM Person WHERE LASTNAME = 'Doe';
```

The same holds for a field named like a keyword: `SELECT date FROM Event` reads the field `date`, while `SELECT DATE FROM Event` reads a field named `DATE`, which no row has. An alias keeps the case it is written in, and a returned row's columns are named by it.


# Authentication

> Authentication methods and identity management in Kinotic.

## Overview

Kinotic supports multiple authentication methods to secure your applications. Every connection to a Kinotic server requires authentication — the platform identifies the caller and establishes a session before any service calls are allowed.

### Authentication Methods

- **Email and Password** — Built-in user management with secure credential storage, offered once your organization admin adds it as one of the application's sign-in providers. Ideal for getting started quickly or for applications that manage their own user base.
- **OIDC Providers** — Connect any standard OpenID Connect provider including Google, Microsoft, Okta, and others. Your organization admin enables OIDC configurations for your application; Google and Microsoft can be managed by Kinotic, with no setup, or use your own credentials.
- **Sign-up** — New people can create their own account, through a provider or with an email and a password verified by email, when the application turns it on.

This page covers what an application developer needs to know. For the platform-level model behind these mechanisms — scope isolation, the `OidcConfiguration` entity, signup and login flows — see [System Security](https://kinotic.ai/platform/system-security) and [Organization Management](https://kinotic.ai/platform/organization-management).

### Scoped Authentication

Authentication happens at the **WebSocket upgrade (handshake)**, not in a STOMP CONNECT frame. Every authentication carries a **scope** that identifies which layer the caller is authenticating against. Scope is structural — it is determined by which of two optional ids are supplied:

<table>
<thead>
  <tr>
    <th>
      <code>
        organizationId
      </code>
    </th>
    
    <th>
      <code>
        applicationId
      </code>
    </th>
    
    <th>
      Resulting scope
    </th>
  </tr>
</thead>

<tbody>
  <tr>
    <td>
      absent
    </td>
    
    <td>
      absent
    </td>
    
    <td>
      <code>
        SYSTEM
      </code>
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      present
    </td>
    
    <td>
      absent
    </td>
    
    <td>
      <code>
        ORGANIZATION
      </code>
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      present
    </td>
    
    <td>
      present
    </td>
    
    <td>
      <code>
        APPLICATION
      </code>
    </td>
  </tr>
</tbody>
</table>

For application developers this is always the `APPLICATION` scope, so both ids are supplied: your organization's id plus your application's id. Scope isolation ensures users are authenticated against the correct user pool — a user in Application A cannot access Application B, even if both applications use the same OIDC provider.

## Connecting with Email and Password

In Node, pass a `BasicCredentialsResolver` carrying the credential and scope values (`clientId`, `clientSecret`, `organizationId`, `applicationId`); they are presented as headers on the WebSocket upgrade:

```typescript
import { BasicCredentialsResolver, Kinotic } from '@kinotic-ai/core'
import { ensureNodeWebSocket } from '@kinotic-ai/core/node'

ensureNodeWebSocket()
await Kinotic.connect({
    credentials: new BasicCredentialsResolver('user@example.com', 'password', 'my-organization', 'my-application')
})
```

The constructor is `BasicCredentialsResolver(clientId, clientSecret, organizationId?, applicationId?)`. The `clientId` is your user's email and `clientSecret` is the password — or a machine identity's id and provisioned secret. The platform looks up the user by email within your application's scope, verifies the password against a securely stored bcrypt hash, and establishes a session.

Your application's users and machines connect to the app server, at your application's API host (the `VITE_KINOTIC_HOST` a UI build receives, `<organizationId>--<applicationId>` under the platform's application domain) or at the app server's own address. The app server authenticates only application identities and the runtime workloads of your organization's applications: organization and system credentials fail there as invalid, and on an application's API host so do the credentials of any other application.

With no `credentials` at all, `Kinotic.connect()` resolves through the default chain: the `KINOTIC_CLIENT_ID` / `KINOTIC_CLIENT_SECRET` (plus optional `KINOTIC_ORGANIZATION_ID` / `KINOTIC_APPLICATION_ID`) environment variables, then the browser session. Server settings resolve the same way — the `server` option, the `KINOTIC_SERVER_HOST/PORT/USE_SSL` variables, the page's own location in a browser, then the management server at `https://api.kinotic.ai`, so an application's client names its API host. To pin the server explicitly, pass it alongside the credentials:

```typescript
await Kinotic.connect({
    server: { host: 'kinotic.example.com', useSSL: true },
    credentials: new BasicCredentialsResolver('user@example.com', 'password', 'my-organization', 'my-application')
})
```

Absent `server` fields fall through to the environment — `{ host }` alone means no TLS and port `58503`, the management server's gateway port, so a connection to a local app server names its port, `58505`.

## Connecting with OIDC

For token-based authentication, pass a Bearer token via `BearerCredentialsResolver`. The resolver sends `Authorization: Bearer <token>` on every (re)connect; pass a supplier function to refresh a short-lived token before each connect:

```typescript
import { BearerCredentialsResolver, Kinotic } from '@kinotic-ai/core'
import { ensureNodeWebSocket } from '@kinotic-ai/core/node'

ensureNodeWebSocket()
await Kinotic.connect({
    credentials: new BearerCredentialsResolver(async () => await getToken())
})
```

A Kinotic-minted JWT already carries the `organizationId` / `applicationId` claims, so no scope headers are needed alongside it. The platform validates the JWT against the OIDC configurations enabled for your application, matches the token's email to a pre-existing user in your application's scope, and establishes a session.

### Browser applications

A browser UI does **not** supply credentials. It signs its user in, or up, over REST at its application's API host, the `VITE_KINOTIC_HOST` of [the UI build contract](https://kinotic.ai/apps/application-structure/applications-and-projects#the-ui-build-contract), which sets a session cookie for that host, then connects to the same host with no credentials — the default resolution finds the session. The host names the application, so the UI never sends its organization or application id. Every call below takes `credentials: 'include'` and is made from a page that is one of the application's own UIs; the API host refuses a sign-in or sign-up from any other page with `403`.

A UI that offers sign-in serves a `/login` page; one that offers sign-up also serves a `/signup` page and the `/signup/verify` page the verification email links to. Both pages start by asking the API host what the login offers:

```text
GET /api/auth/app/login/methods
→ 200 [ { "configurationId": "acme:orders", "type": "PASSWORD", "name": "Email and password", "provider": null, "signUp": true },
        { "configurationId": "4f1c…", "type": "OIDC", "name": "Google", "provider": "google", "signUp": true } ]
```

The answer is the login's sign-in providers, in the order to show them:

<table>
<thead>
  <tr>
    <th>
      Field
    </th>
    
    <th>
      Meaning
    </th>
  </tr>
</thead>

<tbody>
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        type
      </code>
    </td>
    
    <td>
      <code>
        PASSWORD
      </code>
      
      : an email and a password, shown as the password form. <code>
        OIDC
      </code>
      
      : an identity provider, shown as one "Continue with <code>
        name
      </code>
      
      " button, branded by <code>
        provider
      </code>
      
       (<code>
        google
      </code>
      
      , <code>
        azure-ad
      </code>
      
      , <code>
        okta
      </code>
      
      ), which starts a sign-in through <code>
        configurationId
      </code>
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        signUp
      </code>
    </td>
    
    <td>
      New people may sign up: for <code>
        PASSWORD
      </code>
      
      , with an email and a password, so the sign-up page shows its form; for <code>
        OIDC
      </code>
      
      , the provider creates the user of a person it verifies on their first sign-in, so its button belongs on the sign-up page too
    </td>
  </tr>
</tbody>
</table>

A login takes an email and a password only while the application has the **Email and password** provider (a `PasswordConfiguration`, below), so the list has a `PASSWORD` entry; otherwise `POST /api/auth/app/login` and a connection presenting an email and a password answer as for a wrong password.

```typescript
import { Kinotic } from '@kinotic-ai/core'

const env = import.meta.env
const server = { host: env.VITE_KINOTIC_HOST, port: parseInt(env.VITE_KINOTIC_PORT), useSSL: env.VITE_KINOTIC_USE_SSL === 'true' }
const api = `${server.useSSL ? 'https' : 'http'}://${server.host}:${server.port}/api/auth`
const post = (path: string, body: object) => fetch(`${api}${path}`, {
    method: 'POST',
    credentials: 'include',
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
    body: JSON.stringify(body),
})

// what the login offers, for both the /login and the /signup page
const providers = await (await fetch(`${api}/app/login/methods`, { credentials: 'include' })).json()
const password = providers.find(provider => provider.type === 'PASSWORD')

// /login, while the login takes a password: the password form
if ((await post('/app/login', { email, password })).status === 204) {
    await Kinotic.connect({ server })
}

// /login and /signup: one "Continue with <name>" button per provider; on /signup, only those with signUp
async function continueWith(provider: { configurationId: string }) {
    const start = await (await post(`/app/login/oidc/start/${provider.configurationId}`, {})).json()
    window.location.assign(start.redirect)
}

// /signup, while password?.signUp: always answers 202, then the person checks their inbox
await post('/app/signup', { email })

// /signup/verify?token=…: the person chooses a password, and optionally a name, and is signed in
const token = new URLSearchParams(window.location.search).get('token')
const done = await post('/app/signup/complete', { token, password, displayName })
if (done.status === 204) {
    await Kinotic.connect({ server })
}
```

#### Signing in

The login page offers every method the application supports and lets the user choose: the password form, posting to `POST /api/auth/app/login`, which answers `204` with the cookie or a generic `401`, and a button for each provider. A button posts the provider's `id` to `POST /api/auth/app/login/oidc/start/:id`, whose answer carries the `redirect` to send the browser to. The provider returns the browser to `/` on the page that started the sign-in, signed in, or to that page's `/login` with an `error` parameter (`no_user`, `user_exists`, `user_disabled`, `email_not_verified`, `config_not_found`, …). An `email_not_verified` or `no_user` redirect also names the provider by its key in a `provider` parameter (`google`, `azure-ad`, `okta`, …), so the page can tell the user which provider to verify the email with, or which provider's account has no user. No endpoint takes an email before the user has chosen a method, so a login page cannot be used to learn which emails have a user.

`GET /api/auth/me` answers `204` while the page is signed in, and `POST /api/auth/logout` signs it out.

#### Signing up

A person gets a user of your application without an administrator adding them in two ways, each switched on by your organization administrator on the application's sign-in providers:

- **Through a provider.** A provider whose `signUp` is true makes a person it verifies a user on their first sign-in, from the provider's verified email and name. There is no separate sign-up call: the same "Continue with Google" button signs a new person up and an existing user in. A person whose email already has a user under another method is refused with `user_exists`, and signs in the way they did before. Microsoft lets the administrator of any directory set its users' email, so a Microsoft provider that admits every directory — managed by Kinotic, or your own credentials naming `common` or `organizations` — signs up a personal Microsoft account, or a work account whose token carries `xms_edov` (email domain owner verified) or `email_verified` as true; any other Microsoft account is refused with `email_not_verified` and joins by being added or another method. A Microsoft registration of your own emits `xms_edov` once you add it as an optional claim of the ID token in its Entra app registration. A provider naming one directory, your own or a tenant's, signs up that directory's users as its administrator set them.
- **With an email and a password.** While the `PASSWORD` provider's `signUp` is true — the application's **Email and password** provider has `createUserOnSignIn` on — the sign-up page posts `{email}` to `POST /api/auth/app/signup`; the email it sends carries only the application's name and the link. It answers `202` for every email, before anything is sent, and an email that already has a user is sent nothing, so the page cannot learn whether an account exists; tell the person to check their inbox. The email is matched trimmed and lowercased. The email links to `/signup/verify?token=…` on the same UI the sign-up started from and is valid for 24 hours; while a link sent to the address is still valid, asking again sends nothing more, and once it has expired, asking again sends a new one. That page posts `{token, password, displayName}` to `POST /api/auth/app/signup/complete`, where the optional `displayName`, at most 200 characters, is the user's name: it is asked for here, of the person who holds the email, so whoever asked for the link cannot choose it. The call creates the user and answers `204` with the session cookie. It answers `400` for an unknown, used or expired token, or one sent for another application, a missing password or a longer name, `403` from a tenant's site or once the application no longer offers password sign-up, and `409` when the email got a user meanwhile, in which case the person signs in instead.

The sign-up endpoints answer `403` while the application does not offer password sign-up, and from a tenant's site.

Every new user ends up in a tenant. An application signs people up at its own login only while the system manages its tenants (`TenantManagement.SYSTEM`), which gives each new user a tenant of their own; every provider's `signUp` is false at the login of an application whose tenants their administrators manage. There a person joins a tenant by being added to it ([below](#user-management)), or through one of the tenant's own providers that signs people up, at the tenant's login (below).

### Signing in to a tenant

An application whose tenants its administrators manage gives each tenant a login of its own. A page served at one of the tenant's sites, `<tenantId>--<applicationId>--<uiName>` under your organization's subdomain of the sites domain (see [Multi-Tenancy](https://kinotic.ai/apps/persistence/multi-tenancy#tenants-and-their-sites)), signs in to that tenant with the same calls as above: the API host reads the tenant from the page's host, so `/app/login/methods` lists what the tenant's login offers — the tenant's own providers, then the application's — and `/app/login` admits only the tenant's users. Only the tenant's own providers can sign people up there, into the tenant; the application's providers sign in the tenant's existing users, and password sign-up is not offered. The tenant's login takes an email and a password while the tenant's own **Email and password** provider, or the application's, is enabled; a user's password signs in wherever their own tenant's, else the application's, provider is enabled. Deleting the application or the tenant deletes its **Email and password**. A page that is not one of the tenant's sites, such as a UI running locally, names the tenant instead, with `?tenantId=` on the `GET` and the start, and `tenantId` in the login body; the API host answers `404` for a tenant the application does not have, and `403` when a tenant's site names another tenant.

### Sign-in providers

Your organization administrator adds the application's sign-in providers in the portal under the application's **Settings → Sign-in providers** tab, each an `ApplicationOidcConfiguration` (or a `TenantOidcConfiguration` for one tenant's login), or a product built on Kinotic saves them through `OwnedOidcConfigurationService.save`. **Email and password** is a provider of the same list, a `PasswordConfiguration` of the application's login or of one tenant's, saved through `OwnedPasswordConfigurationService.save`: a scope has at most one, `enabled` decides whether its login takes a password, and `createUserOnSignIn`, taken by the application's own only and only while the system manages its tenants, turns on password sign-up. For Google and Microsoft — the kinds `OwnedOidcConfigurationService.findManagedProviders()` lists — each provider chooses whose registration with the provider it signs in through, its `clientRegistrationType`:

<table>
<thead>
  <tr>
    <th>
      <code>
        clientRegistrationType
      </code>
    </th>
    
    <th>
      Setup
    </th>
    
    <th>
      Consent screen
    </th>
  </tr>
</thead>

<tbody>
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        MANAGED
      </code>
      
       — managed by Kinotic
    </td>
    
    <td>
      None: the provider signs in through Kinotic's own registration with Google or Microsoft
    </td>
    
    <td>
      Kinotic's name
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        OWN
      </code>
      
       — your own credentials
    </td>
    
    <td>
      Register an OAuth client at the provider, give the configuration its client ID and secret (and for Microsoft the directory: a tenant id, or <code>
        common
      </code>
      
       / <code>
        organizations
      </code>
      
       for any account), and register the configuration's callback URL, <code>
        https://<organizationId>--<applicationId>.<app API domain>/api/auth/app/login/oidc/callback/<configId>
      </code>
      
      , which the tab shows
    </td>
    
    <td>
      Your application's name and branding
    </td>
  </tr>
</tbody>
</table>

Okta, and Google or Microsoft for one tenant, always use your own credentials. Sign-in and sign-up behave the same either way. Switching a provider between the two is an edit of the same configuration, and its users stay the same users: a user is bound to the identifier the provider gives the person under every client it registers — Google's `sub`, Microsoft's directory and object ids — so a person who signed up under Kinotic's registration signs in under yours, and back. One exception: Microsoft identifies a guest (B2B) user by the directory they sign in to, and Kinotic's registration signs a guest in through their home directory while your own registration naming your directory signs them in through yours. A guest who signed up one way is therefore not recognized the other way, in either direction of a switch: their email already has a user, so the sign-in is refused with `user_exists`, or with `no_user` where the provider does not sign people up. A configuration using Kinotic's registration keeps any client ID and secret it holds, so switching back needs no new setup. Kinotic's registration is shared by every application that uses it, so a user who revokes it at the provider revokes it for all of them.

A provider's `createUserOnSignIn` is its `signUp`: on, it signs new people up where the scope admits them, as described above.

How a sign-in through a provider runs:

1. Your UI renders a button per provider the login offers; the button posts the configuration's id to the start at your API host, whose answer carries the URL to send the browser to
2. The provider returns the browser to the API host, which validates the provider's response, finds the user bound to the identity in your application, or in the tenant the sign-in is to, else claims the pending user an administrator added under the identity's email ([below](#user-management)), else creates it where the provider signs people up, and sets the session cookie. A provider using Kinotic's registration returns the browser to the app server's shared host instead, which validates the response, finds, claims or creates the user, and hands the sign-in to your application's API host under a single-use code, which completes only in the browser that started the sign-in; that host sets the cookie
3. The browser returns to `/` on the site that started the sign-in, which connects with the session; a sign-in that fails returns instead to the `/login` page of that site with an `error` parameter, so every UI that offers sign-in serves a `/login` route. A failure that no longer knows which site started it — the flow's session expired, or a shared registration's single-use code was refused with `handoff_invalid` — returns to the `/login` page of your application's [primary UI](https://kinotic.ai/apps/application-structure/applications-and-projects#applications)

An AI assistant building the pages can ask what the login offers through the `ApplicationService.getLoginMethods` MCP tool, which answers what `GET /api/auth/app/login/methods` answers for the application's own login. Every identity provider is an `OidcConfiguration`, and the email and password a `PasswordConfiguration` — see [System Security](https://kinotic.ai/platform/system-security) for how ownership is captured by the subtype.

## User Management

Besides signing up, an application's users are **added** by an administrator. Your organization administrator manages your application's users on the application's **Users** page in the portal: **Add user**, with the person's email, an optional display name, the tenant they join, picked by searching the application's tenants by the start of a name or id (`TenantService.findForApplicationByPrefix`), and a switch, on by default, that emails them an invitation (`MemberService.addApplicationUser`, taking an `AddApplicationUserRequest` of `email`, `displayName`, `applicationId`, `tenantId` and `sendInvitation`). The person becomes a user of the application at once, with no sign-in method, listed as *Pending* (the user's `pending`, as `MemberService.findApplicationUsers` lists it) until they first sign in, which claims the user in one of two ways:

- **Signing in through one of the application's providers** under the same email, at the application's login or, for a tenant's user, the tenant's: the identity is bound to the user as its first sign-in method, whether or not the provider signs people up. A provider that admits every directory claims the user only under an email the token proves, as for [signing up](#signing-up); a disabled user is refused with `user_disabled`. A user someone already signs in as is not claimed again, and a pending user of one tenant is not claimed at another tenant's login.
- **Accepting the invitation** with a password, where the user's login takes one — their tenant's, else the application's. The accept page sets the password and sends the person to your application's [primary UI](https://kinotic.ai/apps/application-structure/applications-and-projects#applications), where they sign in with that email and password from then on; while the application has no primary UI, the page confirms the user instead. The first UI one of your projects publishes becomes the primary UI unless you have chosen one. The page also names the application's providers and links to the primary UI, where signing in through one of them claims the user as above.

The application must offer a way in before anyone is added: without an invitation, a provider at the user's login — their tenant's own or the application's; with one, a password at that login, or one of the application's own providers and a primary UI, since the invitation links to the primary UI, whose login offers those providers. *Send invitation* later is held to the same rule. Every user belongs to a tenant: an application whose tenants its administrators manage takes one of them, which the administrator must name, and one whose tenants the system manages takes none and gives the person a tenant of their own, as signing up does. *Send invitation* (`MemberService.sendInvitation(email, applicationId)`) sends a pending user the invitation they have again, or a first one; removing a pending user cancels their invitation.

Sign-in and sign-up are configured per application, by the organization in the portal or by any product built on Kinotic through the management API: the application's `PasswordConfiguration`, saved with `OwnedPasswordConfigurationService.save`, turns on sign-in with an email and a password, and with `createUserOnSignIn` sign-up with them, and each provider's `createUserOnSignIn` and `clientRegistrationType`, saved with `OwnedOidcConfigurationService.save`, say whether it signs people up and whose registration it uses. A builder that creates applications for its own users can create each one with `TenantManagement.SYSTEM`, add a Google provider managed by Kinotic with `createUserOnSignIn` on, add an email and a password when the owner wants it, and later save the same provider with `OWN` and the owner's client ID and secret.

For details on user and OIDC configuration management, see the [Organization Management](https://kinotic.ai/platform/organization-management) platform guide.


# Overview

> How services work in Kinotic and the communication patterns they support.

Services are the building blocks of Kinotic applications. Any TypeScript class can be published as a remote service, making its methods callable from any connected client or other service.

## How It Works

1. **Publish** -- Decorate a class with `@Publish` and its methods become remotely callable
2. **Discover** -- The platform automatically registers the service so consumers can reach it by its address
3. **Call** -- Other services and frontends invoke methods through [service proxies](https://kinotic.ai/apps/services/service-proxies) as if they were local

You don't configure routing, serialization, or service discovery. The platform handles all of that.

## Communication Patterns

Kinotic supports two communication patterns.

### Request-Response

Standard RPC. The caller invokes a method and receives a single result as a `Promise`.

```typescript
const result = await greetingService.hello('World')
```

### Streaming

The service pushes multiple values over time. The caller receives an `Observable` and can process each value as it arrives.

```typescript
const stream$ = sensorService.streamReadings('sensor-1')
stream$.subscribe((reading) => console.log(reading))
```

## Service-to-Service Calls

Services can call other services transparently. A published service uses a proxy to another service and invokes it the same way any external client would. The platform routes the call without the caller needing to know where the target service is running.


# Publishing Services

> How to publish TypeScript services in Kinotic using decorators.

Use the `@Publish` decorator to expose any TypeScript class as a remote service. The namespace you pass to `@Publish` combined with the class name forms the service identifier that callers use to reach it.

## Basic Example

```typescript
import { Publish, Version } from '@kinotic-ai/core'

@Version('1.0.0')
@Publish('com.example')
class GreetingService {
    hello(name: string): string {
        return `Hello, ${name}!`
    }

    add(a: number, b: number): number {
        return a + b
    }
}
```

This registers the service as `com.example.GreetingService` at version `1.0.0`, in the zone the client is configured for (see [Zones](#zones) below — an application's services register under its `app.<org>.<app>` zone). Every public method on the class becomes a remotely callable operation.

## Zones

Every service address lives in a zone — the isolation boundary the gateway validates on each call (see [CRI Format](https://kinotic.ai/platform/reference/cri-format)). An application's services always register inside the application's own zone: the client's `zonePrefix` is set from static project configuration before services are instantiated, and declared zones are appended to it, so a service can never register outside its application.

```typescript
import { Kinotic } from '@kinotic-ai/core'
import { appZone } from '@kinotic-ai/management-api'
import config from './.config/kinotic.config'

// In your application's entry point, before any @Publish class is instantiated
Kinotic.zonePrefix = appZone(config.organizationId, config.applicationId)
```

`@Publish` classes may be instantiated before or after `Kinotic.connect()`: a
registration made before the connection is up queues and subscribes once it is, and
every registration re-subscribes automatically on reconnect — including across an
explicit `disconnect()` / `connect()` cycle.

```typescript
@Publish()                       // → srv://app.acme-org.orders-app~OrderService
class OrderService { ... }

@Zone('billing')                 // → srv://app.acme-org.orders-app.billing~InvoiceService
@Publish()
class InvoiceService { ... }
```

A default zone for every service in the project can also be declared in `package.json`; a class-level `@Zone` overrides it:

```json
{ "kinotic": { "zone": "billing" } }
```

```typescript
import pkg from './package.json' with { type: 'json' }
Kinotic.defaultZone = pkg.kinotic?.zone ?? null
```

The gateway rejects any send or subscribe outside the zones the authenticated participant may address, so a wrong or missing zone routes nowhere — it can never reach another application.

## Registering on a specific client

`@Publish` registers every instance with the global `Kinotic` client. A service hosted on a client you created yourself — a second `KinoticSingleton`, connected under its own credentials or to another server — is registered through that client's `serviceRegistry` with a `ServiceIdentifier` naming the namespace, the service name, and the full zone:

```typescript
import { KinoticSingleton, ServiceIdentifier } from '@kinotic-ai/core'

const host = new KinoticSingleton()
await host.connect({ server: { host: 'localhost', port: 58505 }, credentials })   // the app server

const identifier = new ServiceIdentifier('com.example', 'GreetingService', 'app.acme-org.orders-app')
host.serviceRegistry.register(identifier, new GreetingService())   // → srv://app.acme-org.orders-app~com.example.GreetingService

// later, when the service should no longer be reachable
host.serviceRegistry.unRegister(identifier)
```

The zone is the complete zone the service lives in: `zonePrefix` and `defaultZone` apply to `@Publish` classes only. Registering the same identifier twice on one client is a no-op, and `unRegister` ends any stream the service is still producing with an error to its caller.

## The service directory

Every published class under the project's `servicesPaths` gets a service definition from `kinotic generate` and `kinotic sync`, its functions with their parameters and types, written to the `ServiceDefinitions` module under `generatedPath`. A project that imports that module has the runtime register each service in the platform's service directory as the service comes online: the services registered before `connect` when the client connects, and a service registered on a connected client as it registers. Only a service in an application's zone, `app.<organizationId>.<applicationId>` or a zone under it, is registered, through the platform's `ApplicationServiceDirectory` in `app-api`, which refuses a zone that is not the application's or an application outside the caller's organization. The directory then holds the application's services beside the platform's own, with their liveness; a service the project declares no definition for serves on its zone alone. A definition naming other functions than the class serves fails the registration, and with it the connection, until `kinotic sync` runs again.

### Parameter and return types

Arguments and results travel as JSON, so a function's types are published as JSON carries them:

- A `Promise` or `PromiseLike` result is asynchronous and an `Observable` result is a stream, of the type it resolves to or emits.
- `any`, `unknown`, and a type parameter with no constraint accept anything; a constrained type parameter is its constraint.
- Interfaces, classes (their fields, without their methods), generic instantiations such as `Page<Report>`, mapped types such as `Partial<Report>` and `Pick<Report, 'id'>`, intersections, and unions of objects are objects, named for the type and its type arguments (`Page_Report`, `Partial_Report`).
- `Record<string, V>` and `{[key: string]: V}` are maps, enums are enums, and a union of string literals is a string.
- A `Date` is published as a date, but it arrives as the ISO-8601 string a date travels as: the service receives a string, and a TypeScript caller gets a string back. `kinotic generate` logs a warning for each one, and the directory carries the same warning in the `warnings` metadata of the parameter, or of the function for a result.
- A `Map`, `Set`, `Uint8Array`, `Buffer`, `bigint`, tuple, or function fails generation with the reason and the type to declare instead.

## Decorators

### @Publish(namespace?, name?, advertise?)

Marks a class for publication. The full service identifier becomes `namespace.ClassName`; both parts are optional (the name defaults to the class name). A service published with no namespace is addressed by its name in its zone, `srv://<zone>~ClassName`, and the platform's service directory names it in its zone's namespace, `<zone>.ClassName`, so services of the same name in different applications stay apart. Passing `advertise` as `true` additionally advertises the service in the platform service directory, so it appears in directory listings for browsing and invocation — publishing alone makes a service callable over RPC without listing it.

### @Zone(zone)

Declares the zone the service is addressable in, relative to the client's `zonePrefix`. The zone is one or more dot-separated labels of lowercase letters, digits, and interior dashes.

### @Version(version)

Sets the semantic version for the service in `X.Y.Z` format. Callers can pin to a specific version when resolving the service.

### @Scope

A getter or method decorator that marks the member providing the scope identifier. Scope targets requests at one specific instance of a service — for example the copy running on a particular node or device.

```typescript
import { Publish, Scope } from '@kinotic-ai/core'

@Publish('com.example')
class DeviceService {
    deviceId: string

    @Scope
    get scope(): string {
        return this.deviceId
    }

    constructor(deviceId: string) {
        this.deviceId = deviceId
    }

    getStatus(): string {
        return `Status for device ${this.deviceId}`
    }
}
```

When a caller targets a specific scope (e.g., `device-42`), the platform routes the request to the instance whose `deviceId` matches.

### @Context

A method decorator that marks a method as receiving the request context: a `ServiceContext` carrying the calling participant — the same caller a Java service receives as its `Participant` parameter — plus whatever a registered `ContextInterceptor` adds.

**The context parameter must be the method's final parameter.** Callers never pass it — the platform appends it after the caller-supplied arguments.

```typescript
import { Publish, Context, type ServiceContext } from '@kinotic-ai/core'
import { isOrganizationParticipant, requireParticipant } from '@kinotic-ai/management-api'

@Publish('com.example')
class OrderService {
    @Context
    async listOrders(status: string, context: ServiceContext): Promise<Order[]> {
        const caller = requireParticipant(context.participant, isOrganizationParticipant)
        return this.orders.findByOrganization(caller.organizationId, status)
    }
}
```

`context.participant` is the participant the gateway authenticated on the calling connection, serialized with its scope discriminator and ids (`type`, `organizationId`, `applicationId`). It is absent only for an invocation that originated inside the platform with no participant bound, such as a scheduled job.

`requireParticipant` is the counterpart of a Java service's `securityContext.requireParticipant(OrganizationParticipant.class)`: it returns the participant narrowed by the guard you pass (`isSystemParticipant`, `isOrganizationParticipant`, or `isApplicationParticipant`), throws if the invocation carries no participant, and fails the invocation with an `AuthorizationException` — the same name a Java refusal carries — when the caller does not hold that scope. The guards alone narrow without throwing, for a method that serves more than one scope.

A `ContextInterceptor` registered through `Kinotic.serviceRegistry.registerContextInterceptor(...)` receives the context with the participant already set and returns the context the method sees, so it can add data derived from the caller or from the request headers:

```typescript
Kinotic.serviceRegistry.registerContextInterceptor({
    async intercept(event, context) {
        return { ...context, tenant: await tenants.forParticipant(context.participant) }
    }
})
```


# Service Proxies

> How to call remote services using service proxies in Kinotic.

Service proxies let you call remote services as if they were local objects. You define a typed interface, create a class that implements it, and delegate calls to the remote service through the Kinotic connection.

## Writing a Service Proxy

The pattern is:

1. Define an interface describing the service methods
2. Create a class that implements the interface
3. In the constructor, obtain a proxy via `kinotic.serviceProxy()`
4. Implement methods by calling `invoke()` or `invokeStream()` on the proxy

### Example

```typescript
import type { IKinotic, IServiceProxy } from '@kinotic-ai/core'
import type { Observable } from 'rxjs'

export interface INotificationService {
    sendAlert(message: string): Promise<void>
    watchAlerts(severity: string): Observable<Alert>
}

export class NotificationService implements INotificationService {

    private readonly serviceProxy: IServiceProxy

    constructor(kinotic: IKinotic) {
        // A proxy targets the service's full address, including its zone (see CRI Format).
        // A platform service is reached in management-api or app-api; an application's own service
        // is reached in its app zone, e.g. app.acme-org.orders-app~com.example.NotificationService
        this.serviceProxy = kinotic.serviceProxy('app.acme-org.orders-app~com.example.NotificationService')
    }

    sendAlert(message: string): Promise<void> {
        return this.serviceProxy.invoke('sendAlert', [message])
    }

    watchAlerts(severity: string): Observable<Alert> {
        return this.serviceProxy.invokeStream('watchAlerts', [severity])
    }
}
```

### Usage

```typescript
import { Kinotic } from '@kinotic-ai/core'

const notifications = new NotificationService(Kinotic)

// Request-response
await notifications.sendAlert('High CPU usage detected')

// Streaming (returns an Observable)
notifications.watchAlerts('critical').subscribe((alert) => {
    console.log('Alert:', alert)
})
```

## Invocation Methods

Each proxy provides two ways to call the remote service:

<table>
<thead>
  <tr>
    <th>
      Method
    </th>
    
    <th>
      Returns
    </th>
    
    <th>
      Use When
    </th>
  </tr>
</thead>

<tbody>
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        invoke(method, args?)
      </code>
    </td>
    
    <td>
      <code>
        Promise<any>
      </code>
    </td>
    
    <td>
      The service returns a single result
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        invokeStream(method, args?)
      </code>
    </td>
    
    <td>
      <code>
        Observable<any>
      </code>
    </td>
    
    <td>
      The service pushes multiple values over time
    </td>
  </tr>
</tbody>
</table>


# Streaming

> Real-time data streaming between services and clients.

Kinotic services can push multiple values to callers over time using the streaming pattern. Instead of returning a single response, a streaming method returns an `Observable` that emits values as they become available.

## Defining a Streaming Method

Any service method that returns an `Observable` is treated as a streaming endpoint.

```typescript
import { Publish } from '@kinotic-ai/core'
import { Observable, interval } from 'rxjs'
import { map } from 'rxjs/operators'

@Publish('com.example')
class SensorService {
    streamReadings(sensorId: string): Observable<SensorReading> {
        return interval(1000).pipe(
            map(() => ({
                sensorId,
                value: Math.random() * 100,
                timestamp: new Date().toISOString()
            }))
        )
    }
}
```

## Consuming a Stream

Callers receive an `Observable` and subscribe to process values as they arrive.

```typescript
const stream$ = sensorService.streamReadings('sensor-1')

const subscription = stream$.subscribe({
    next: (reading) => console.log('Reading:', reading.value),
    error: (err) => console.error('Stream error:', err),
    complete: () => console.log('Stream ended')
})

// Stop listening when done
subscription.unsubscribe()
```

## How a Stream Ends

A stream ends for its caller in one of five ways, and the service stops producing in every one of them:

- **The service completes it.** The caller's `Observable` completes.
- **The service fails it.** The caller's `Observable` errors with the exception the service threw or emitted.
- **The caller unsubscribes.** A cancel reaches the service, which unsubscribes from the `Observable` the method returned, so a finite source stops early and an `interval` stops ticking.
- **The caller falls too far behind a stream that cannot be suspended.** The caller's `Observable` errors with `RpcStreamOverflowException` (see [A Caller That Falls Behind](#a-caller-that-falls-behind)).
- **The caller is gone.** The platform watches the caller's reply destination for every stream in progress, on the node hosting a Java service and on the gateway for a TypeScript one. When nothing listens there any more — the caller's connection closed, or its node left the cluster — the stream is cancelled the same way an unsubscribe cancels it. A TypeScript service whose own connection ends, however it ends, cancels every stream it was producing at that moment, because the gateway has already failed those callers (see [service call liveness](https://kinotic.ai/platform/service-call-liveness)).

A service that stops while producing a stream ends it with an error at the caller rather than a silent cancel.

## A Caller That Falls Behind

A caller connected through the gateway, such as a browser, the CLI or a TypeScript service, receives a stream only as fast as its connection takes it. The gateway counts what it has written to the connection that the socket has not sent yet. When that backlog passes 1 MiB, the gateway suspends each stream to the connection that can be suspended, as its next value arrives, and resumes them all once the backlog drains below 256 KiB. Values already on their way when the suspend went out still arrive, so the caller loses nothing and receives every value in order.

A stream produced by a Java service can be suspended. Once the suspend reaches the service, it sends nothing more until it is resumed, and its source has been asked for at most 32 values the service has not sent. A source that produces only as fast as it is asked stops there, whether it emits synchronously or not: `Flux.range`, `Flux.fromIterable`, `Flux.generate`, a database cursor, or a `Flux.create` that reads `onRequest`. A source emitting on the service's own event loop also yields the loop every 16 values, so a long synchronous stream does not hold it.

A source that produces on its own schedule does not wait to be asked. Once its caller has been behind long enough to use up those 32 values, what happens depends on the source:

<table>
<thead>
  <tr>
    <th>
      Source
    </th>
    
    <th>
      While its caller is behind
    </th>
  </tr>
</thead>

<tbody>
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        Flux.interval
      </code>
    </td>
    
    <td>
      fails the stream with an overflow error
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        Flux.create
      </code>
      
      , by default
    </td>
    
    <td>
      keeps buffering inside the service, without limit
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        Sinks.many().multicast().directBestEffort()
      </code>
    </td>
    
    <td>
      drops the values for that caller, who never sees them
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      a <code>
        share()
      </code>
      
       or <code>
        publish()
      </code>
      
       of one source
    </td>
    
    <td>
      pauses every caller of the shared source, since it emits only as fast as its slowest subscriber asks
    </td>
  </tr>
</tbody>
</table>

Give a stream like these an overflow strategy that says what its caller misses while it is behind: `onBackpressureLatest()` keeps only the newest value, `onBackpressureDrop()` drops values until the caller catches up, and `onBackpressureBuffer(maxSize)` holds up to `maxSize` values and fails the stream with an overflow error past them. Apply it to each caller's stream, after any `share()`, so one slow caller does not hold back the others:

```java
@Override
public Flux<Reading> streamReadings(String sensorId) {
    return readings.share()                                  // one subscription to the sensor feed
                   .filter(reading -> reading.sensorId().equals(sensorId))
                   .onBackpressureLatest();                  // a caller that falls behind skips to the newest reading
}
```

A stream produced by a TypeScript service cannot be suspended. The gateway logs a warning when its caller falls behind, and once 32 MiB of that stream's own values are waiting to be sent it cancels the stream at the service and fails it at the caller with `RpcStreamOverflowException`, so the caller can request it again. A backlog the connection's other streams built up never cancels it. A stream that declared it can be suspended but keeps sending more than 5 seconds after a suspend is treated the same way, with a warning that names it.

The gateway sends every suspend, resume and cancel to the address the caller sent its request to, whatever the stream's values say about where they came from.

## Use Cases

- **Real-time data feeds** -- IoT sensors, live metrics, dashboards
- **Notifications and alerts** -- Push updates to connected clients
- **Change data capture** -- React to data changes as they happen
- **Large result sets** -- Stream results incrementally instead of loading everything at once


# Introduction

> Learn what Kinotic is, why it exists, and how it helps developers and AI agents build enterprise-grade applications at scale.

Kinotic is a next-generation cloud operating system that abstracts away infrastructure complexity so developers and AI agents can focus on what matters: building great applications.

## Humane Representation of Thought

The rise of AI-assisted development has unlocked a new paradigm -- rapid iteration driven by natural-language intent and intelligent code generation. Kinotic is purpose-built for this paradigm. Whether a human developer or an AI agent is writing the code, Kinotic provides the guardrails, services, and runtime that turn quick prototypes into production-grade systems.

## Core Components

- **Kinotic Apps** -- Applications that run on Kinotic OS. Today, Kinotic Apps are built with TypeScript running on Bun -- you write standard TypeScript for domain models, business logic, and UI, and the platform handles infrastructure, deployment, and scaling. Support for Go, Java, and Python backends is coming soon.
- **Kinotic OS** -- The cloud operating system that runs your apps. It provides authentication, authorization, persistence, service mesh, observability, and deployment infrastructure out of the box.
- **Kinotic OS Cloud** -- A fully managed SaaS offering of Kinotic OS. No servers to provision, no infrastructure to maintain.
- **Kinotic CLI** -- The developer tool that ties it all together. Use it to initialize projects, define entities, generate service code, and deploy applications.

## Why Kinotic?

**Rapid prototyping.** Go from an idea to a running application in minutes with the CLI and generated services.

**Enterprise-ready.** Software bill of materials and full observability mean you never have to rewrite for production.

**Internet scale.** The platform is designed to scale horizontally from day one.

## What These Docs Cover

This documentation walks through everything you need to build and ship a Kinotic App:

1. **Quick Start** -- Run Kinotic on your machine and build your first app with Claude Code.
2. **Application Structure** -- Understand how organizations, applications, projects, and artifacts fit together.
3. **Services** -- Publish and consume services across your application.
4. **Persistence** -- Define entities, configure indexes, and run queries.
5. **Security** -- Set up authentication and authorization.
6. **Deployment** -- Ship your application to Kinotic OS or Kinotic OS Cloud.

Ready to build something? Head to the [Quick Start](https://kinotic.ai/getting-started/quick-start) to create your first Kinotic App.


# Quick Start

> Run Kinotic on your own machine, create your organization, and build your first app with Claude Code.

Kinotic runs on your own machine today. Kinotic OS Cloud, where Kinotic runs for you, is coming soon.

<tabs sync="kinotic-install">
<tabs-item icon="i-lucide-laptop" label="Local">

The local install runs the whole of Kinotic OS in Docker on your machine: its servers, the portal, the
Git server that holds your projects' repositories, and the storage your apps' data and UIs live in.
Nothing leaves your machine except the downloads.

#### Prerequisites

- **Docker** with Compose, running, with at least 12 GB of memory available to it
- **Node.js** 18 or later, which the Kinotic CLI runs on
- **macOS on Apple silicon, or Linux with KVM** (`/dev/kvm`), where your apps' deployments run as micro VMs
- **Claude Code**, which builds your app with the Kinotic plugin
- An internet connection for the first start, which downloads Kinotic, and for each new project, whose starting code comes from GitHub

<steps level="4">

#### Install and launch Kinotic

```bash
curl -fsSL https://kinotic.ai/install | sh
```

This installs [Bun](https://bun.sh) if you don't have it, installs the Kinotic CLI, and runs
`kinotic local up`, which starts Kinotic and the node your projects deploy to. The first start downloads
everything and prepares the database, which takes a few minutes; the command returns once Kinotic is
ready. With the CLI already installed, `kinotic local up` alone starts it.

#### Create your organization

Open [http://localhost:9090/signup](http://localhost:9090/signup), enter your name and email, then name
your organization and set a password. A local install sends no email, so the page goes straight on, and
you are signed in to your new organization.

#### Follow the Quickstart in the portal

Open **Quickstart** in the portal's sidebar. It walks you through installing the Kinotic plugin in Claude
Code, connecting Claude to your local Kinotic, and asking for your app. Claude creates the application
and its project, writes the entities, services and UIs, and pushes to the project's repository; every
push deploys.

</steps>

`kinotic local down` stops Kinotic and the apps it deployed, and keeps your data for the next `kinotic local up`;
`kinotic local down --delete-data` deletes it. `kinotic local status` and `kinotic local logs` show what
it is doing, and the [CLI reference](https://kinotic.ai/apps/cli-reference#kinotic-local) covers each command.
[Developing Kinotic](https://kinotic.ai/platform/contributing) covers how to work on Kinotic itself.

</tabs-item>

<tabs-item icon="i-lucide-cloud" label="Cloud">
<cloud-waitlist>



</cloud-waitlist>
</tabs-item>
</tabs>

## What's Next?

Once your first app is deployed, explore the rest of the documentation:

- [Application Structure](https://kinotic.ai/apps/application-structure/overview) -- Understand how organizations, applications, projects, and artifacts are organized.
- [Services](https://kinotic.ai/apps/services/overview) -- Learn how to publish and consume services across your application.
- [Persistence](https://kinotic.ai/apps/persistence/overview) -- Dive deeper into entity definitions, relationships, and querying.


# Authentication Providers

> Let your organization's members sign in to the Kinotic portal with your own identity provider.

An **authentication provider** is an identity provider, such as Okta or a Microsoft Entra ID directory, that your organization's members use to sign in to the Kinotic portal.

You add providers in the Kinotic portal under **Organization settings > Authentication providers**. Each provider is offered on your organization's login page once its **callback URL** is registered at the provider.

## Setup order

Every provider follows the same order:

1. Create an application (client) registration at the provider and note its client ID and secret.
2. Add the provider in Kinotic. Kinotic creates the configuration and shows its exact callback URL.
3. Register that callback URL as a redirect URI at the provider.

The callback URL contains the configuration's id, which is only created when you first save the provider in Kinotic. That is why the provider registration is created first with a placeholder redirect URI and updated afterwards.

## Guides

- [Okta SSO setup](https://kinotic.ai/organizations/okta-sso-setup)


# Okta SSO Setup

> Configure Okta as a single sign-on provider for your Kinotic organization.

This guide connects an Okta org to your Kinotic organization so members can sign in to the Kinotic portal with **Sign in with Okta**.

The setup goes back and forth once: you create the app in Okta, add the provider in Kinotic, then copy Kinotic's callback URL back into Okta.

## Prerequisites

- Administrator access to your **Okta Admin Console** (for example `https://yourorg-admin.okta.com`).
- Administrator access to your **Kinotic organization**.

## 1. Create the app integration in Okta

1. In the Okta Admin Console, go to **Applications > Applications** and click **Create App Integration**.
2. Select the **Classic experience** tab, choose **OIDC - OpenID Connect** as the sign-in method, and **Web Application** as the application type. Click **Next**.

![Create app integration dialog](https://kinotic.ai/images/docs/okta/01-create-app-integration.png)

![OIDC - OpenID Connect and Web Application selected](https://kinotic.ai/images/docs/okta/02-oidc-web-application.png)

1. Enter an **App integration name**, for example `Kinotic`, and under **Client definition** choose **Use Okta-generated client ID**.

![App integration name](https://kinotic.ai/images/docs/okta/03-app-name.png)

1. Under **Grant type**, keep **Authorization Code** checked.
2. Leave **Sign-in redirect URIs** as Okta's placeholder (`http://localhost:8080/authorization-code/callback`) for now. You will replace it with Kinotic's callback URL in step 4.

![Grant type and redirect URIs](https://kinotic.ai/images/docs/okta/04-grant-type-redirect-uris.png)

1. Under **Assignments**, choose **Allow everyone in your organization to access**, or **Limit access to selected groups** to restrict who can sign in. Click **Save**.

![Assignments](https://kinotic.ai/images/docs/okta/05-assignments.png)

## 2. Copy the client credentials

On the saved app's **General** tab, find **Client Credentials**:

- Copy the **Client ID**.
- Under **Client Secrets**, use the copy button to copy the secret.

![Client credentials](https://kinotic.ai/images/docs/okta/06-client-credentials.png)

<alert type="warning">

Treat the client secret like a password. Paste it directly into Kinotic; don't share it in chat or screenshots.

</alert>

## 3. Add the provider in Kinotic

1. In the Kinotic portal, open **Organization settings** and select the **Authentication providers** tab. Click **Add provider**.

![Authentication providers tab](https://kinotic.ai/images/docs/okta/07-kinotic-providers-empty.png)

1. Fill in the form:

    </th>

        Okta
      </code>

      <strong>

       -- no <code>

       and no path

      </strong>

      The client ID from Okta

        aud
      </code>
      
       claim of Okta's tokens is not the client ID
    </td>

![Add provider form](https://kinotic.ai/images/docs/okta/08-kinotic-add-provider.png)

![Advanced section with Audience](https://kinotic.ai/images/docs/okta/09-kinotic-add-provider-advanced.png)

1. Click **Add provider**.

Kinotic creates the configuration and the drawer shows two URLs, each with a copy button:

- **Callback URL** -- `https://<api-host>/api/auth/org/login/sso/callback/<config-id>`
- **Direct sign-in link** -- `https://<api-host>/api/auth/org/login/<org>/start/<config-id>`, useful for a tile in Okta's app launcher.

Copy the **Callback URL**.

![Provider added with callback URL](https://kinotic.ai/images/docs/okta/10-kinotic-callback-url.png)

<alert type="info">

The configuration id at the end of the callback URL is created on the first save, so the callback URL only exists after you click **Add provider**.

</alert>

## 4. Register the callback URL in Okta

1. Back in Okta, open the app's **General** tab, and click **Edit** on **General Settings**.
2. Under **LOGIN**, replace the **Sign-in redirect URIs** placeholder with the callback URL you copied from Kinotic.
3. Click **Save**.

![Sign-in redirect URI saved](https://kinotic.ai/images/docs/okta/11-okta-redirect-uri-saved.png)

<alert type="warning">

Okta matches redirect URIs exactly. Paste the whole callback URL, including the configuration id at the end.

</alert>

The provider now appears as **Enabled** in Kinotic:

![Okta provider enabled](https://kinotic.ai/images/docs/okta/12-kinotic-provider-enabled.png)

## 5. Give people access

Okta decides who may authenticate, and Kinotic decides who belongs to your organization. An Okta sign-in gets in only when it matches a member of your organization, so assigning someone to the Okta app alone does not let them in.

- **New members.** In Kinotic, open **Members** and click **Add member**, using the email address the person has in Okta. With **Send an invitation email** off, their first **Sign in with Okta** admits them: Kinotic matches the email Okta verified to the member you added and links their Okta account to it.
- **People who already sign in.** Someone who already signs in to your organization another way, such as you after creating the organization with GitHub, is not matched by email. They sign in as they do now, open **Profile**, and under **Sign-in methods** choose Okta from **Connect another way to sign in**. From then on, either method signs them in.

Each person must also be assigned to the Okta app in Okta, as set up in step 1.

## 6. Test sign-in

1. Open your organization's login page, `https://<portal-host>/login/<org>`. It now shows **Sign in with Okta** (using your display name).
2. Sign in as one of the people from step 5.

# Overview

> Set up a Kinotic organization -- its members, how they sign in, and the Apps it builds.

An **organization** is the top-level home for everything you build on Kinotic. It owns its members, the identity providers they sign in with, and its [Apps](https://kinotic.ai/apps/application-structure/overview).

Organization administrators manage the organization from **Organization settings** in the Kinotic portal.

## Organization setup

- **Authentication providers** -- let your members sign in to the portal with your company's identity provider, such as Okta.
- **Apps** -- build, publish, and deploy applications inside the organization.

For how organizations, users, and OIDC configurations work under the hood, see [Organization Management](https://kinotic.ai/platform/organization-management).


# System Architecture

> High-level architecture of the Kinotic OS platform.

## Overview

Kinotic OS is a full-stack application platform that handles service communication, persistence, authentication, authorization, deployment, and observability. The system is composed of several core components that work together to provide a seamless development and runtime experience.

## Core Components

- **Management server** (`kinotic-server-management`) — The API the portal, the Kinotic CLI and organization members' MCP hosts call: sign-up, logins and invitations, the `management-api` services, and the GitHub App's webhook.
- **System server** (`kinotic-server-system`) — The API the system console and the vm-managers call: the `system-api` services, project deployments, and the cluster singletons that reconcile deployments and delete old workload runs.
- **App server** (`kinotic-server-app`) — The API every application's users, UIs and microservices call: the `app-api` persistence services and the services applications publish in their own zones, each application at its own API host.
- **RPC Gateway** — Each server's gateway routes remote procedure calls between its clients and published services over STOMP/WebSocket, and serves the server's REST and MCP endpoints.
- **Persistence Layer** — Provides automatic CRUD operations for entities backed by Elasticsearch.
- **Auth System** — Handles authentication (email/password and OIDC) across three authorization hierarchies: System, Organization, and Application. Each server admits only the participants it serves.

The three servers are Spring Boot applications that form one Ignite cluster, in which each hosts only its own zones. [Defense in Depth](https://kinotic.ai/platform/defense-in-depth#network-architecture) shows which participants each admits and which zones each hosts.

## Communication

Services communicate via STOMP over WebSocket, with messages routed by CRI (Kinotic Resource Identifier). Each service, method, and event stream is addressable through a CRI, which follows the format:

```text
scheme://[scope@]resourceName[/path][#version]
```

The RPC gateway uses CRIs to route requests to the correct service instance, apply versioning, and enforce scope-based multi-tenancy. See the [CRI Format](https://kinotic.ai/platform/reference/cri-format) reference for details.

### Kinotic RPC on its own

Kinotic RPC, the service and event layer in `kinotic-core` and `kinotic-api-gateway`, runs without the rest of
Kinotic OS. A server built on it alone supplies two beans the gateway authenticates and authorizes every
connection with:

<table>
<thead>
  <tr>
    <th>
      Bean
    </th>
    
    <th>
      What it decides
    </th>
  </tr>
</thead>

<tbody>
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        SecurityService
      </code>
    </td>
    
    <td>
      Who a connection is: it authenticates the STOMP CONNECT headers and returns the connection's <code>
        Participant
      </code>
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        ZoneRulesResolver
      </code>
    </td>
    
    <td>
      What that participant may address: the <code>
        ZoneRules
      </code>
      
       of zones it may send to and subscribe in, which the gateway narrows to the zones the server's <code>
        ZonePartitioningService
      </code>
      
       serves
    </td>
  </tr>
</tbody>
</table>

Kinotic OS's servers supply each from their own module: the `SecurityService` of the server, and kinotic-domain's
resolver, which gives system, organization and application participants their zones.

### Never block the event loop

A Java service published with `@Publish` is invoked on a Vert.x event loop it shares with the other services on the node, the same rule Vert.x sets for its own handlers. A method returns a `Future`, `CompletableFuture`, `Mono` or `Flux` and lets the work complete off the loop; a method that is slow, because it blocks on a synchronous client, a lock or a sleep, or because it does heavy CPU work, hands that work off inside itself:

```java
@Override
public Future<Report> render(String id) {
    return vertx.executeBlocking(() -> renderer.render(id));   // the loop is free while the worker runs
}
```

The platform never hands off on a service's behalf. A method that blocks stalls every service sharing its loop, and Vert.x's blocked-thread checker reports it in the log.


# Configuration

> Configuration reference for Kinotic OS server and services.

<alert type="info">

Configuration reference coming soon.

</alert>

## Overview

Kinotic OS is configured through a combination of application properties, environment variables, and Helm chart values. Key configuration areas include:

- **Server configuration** — Port bindings, cluster discovery, and runtime settings
- **Elasticsearch settings** — Connection URLs, index defaults, and replica configuration
- **Authentication** — OIDC provider configuration, session management, and security policies
- **Environment variables** — Runtime overrides for containerized deployments
- **Helm values** — Kubernetes-specific configuration for resource limits, replicas, ingress, and TLS

## Loki, Tempo, and Mimir

The server reads workload logs from Grafana Loki, and workload traces and metrics from Grafana Tempo and Mimir (see [Observability](https://kinotic.ai/platform/observability#workload-logs)). Each runs multi-tenant, and the server queries the tenant the caller may see.

In docker-compose the server points at `http://loki:3100`, `http://tempo:3200`, and `http://mimir:9009`; the Helm chart defaults them to `http://loki.observability.svc:3100`, `http://tempo.observability.svc:3100`, and `http://mimir.observability.svc:9009`, the services the Azure terraform deploys in the `observability` namespace (Tempo's chart serves its HTTP API on 3100).

Every server also runs the OpenTelemetry Java agent its image embeds, which exports the server's own traces and metrics to the system tenant, `kinotic-system`, read by the system console's System **Observability** page. The Helm chart attaches it on every server and sends each signal straight to its store, with no collector between; its logs reach Loki through Alloy instead, so the agent exports none:

## VM provider

Each vm-manager node runs every workload on one VM provider, chosen by the node rather than by the workloads it is given. The node reports which one it runs when it registers, and the orchestrator surfaces it on the node in the system UI.

<table>
<thead>

      </code>

    </td>

      libkrun micro VM, one per workload
    </td>

    <td>
      <code>
        CLOUD_HYPERVISOR
      </code>
    </td>

      Linux nodes provisioned with Docker and Kata Containers
    </td>

      Cloud Hypervisor micro VM, one per workload
    </td>
  </tr>
</tbody>

`CLOUD_HYPERVISOR` needs the node's Docker daemon to register a `kata-clh` runtime and to keep its data root on an XFS filesystem mounted with `prjquota`. Without the quota support the daemon refuses any workload declaring a `diskSizeMb`, since that is what caps a container's rootfs. `deployment/vm-node` in the repository provisions a node that way and installs the vm-manager as a service.

`BOXLITE` keeps box records and every guest's rootfs disk under one directory. That directory is the filesystem workload disks grow into and the one the node reports its `totalDiskMb` from, so a node taking workloads of any size wants it on a data volume rather than the root filesystem under the service account's home.

<thead>
  <tr>
    <th>

    </th>

    </th>
    
    <th>

    </th>
  </tr>
</thead>

<tbody>
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        BOXLITE_HOME
      </code>
      
       (vm-manager)
    </td>

    </td>

      <code>
