# Grind Jobs

> The declarative job framework for long-running platform work.

## Overview

Grind (the `kinotic-grind` module) is the platform's job framework: multi-step work such as a project deployment or a provisioning pipeline, expressed as a **job** of **tasks** that share a scope. Its core idea is declarative state injection — instead of threading an ever-growing context object through every step, each task declares what it consumes, injected from the job scope, and what it produces, stored back under a `Store`. Every run is recorded, resumable after a failure, and observable as a live event stream.

## Defining a job

A `JobDefinition` is built fluently. Tasks execute in the order they are added, and each task's result is kept according to the `Store` the task declares:

```java
JobDefinition job = JobDefinition.create("Deploy project")
        .name("project-deploy").version("1")
        .input(project)                       // seeds the scope before the first task
        .task(Tasks.fromCallable("Resolve deploy target", new Callable<DeployTarget>() {

            @Autowired
            private Project project;          // injected from the job scope

            @Override
            public DeployTarget call() {
                return resolveTarget(project);
            }
        }).store(Store.state("deployTarget")))
        .task(Tasks.fromCallable("Sync project source", new Callable<String>() {

            @Autowired
            private DeployTarget target;      // stored by the previous task

            @Override
            public String call() {
                return syncSource(target);
            }
        }));
```

`name` and `version` identify the job across runs and are required to run it. `input(...)` stores values in the scope as beans, so the first task's dependencies resolve the same way as any other.

Definitions nest: `jobDefinition(...)` adds a whole `JobDefinition` as one task of another. A nested definition declares a `JobScope` — `CHILD` (the default) gives it a scope of its own that is destroyed when it finishes, while `PARENT` lets it store directly into its parent's scope. Passing `parallel = true` to `JobDefinition.create` makes the definition's tasks execute concurrently; the first failure cancels the in-flight siblings.

### Task factories

The `Tasks` class adapts plain functional types into tasks. Each factory takes what every task needs, its description and its work; everything else is set with the fluent methods of the returned `Task`. A `Task` is immutable: each fluent method returns a copy, so one instance can be added to several definitions, or serve as a step and as another step's reload task, without either seeing the other's settings. The instance-taking factories inject the given instance's `@Autowired` and `@Value` members against the job scope before each invocation, so one instance serves one execution at a time; a task that runs concurrently, in a parallel definition or in concurrent runs, is built with `Tasks.fromClass`, which constructs an instance per execution:

- `Tasks.fromCallable(description, callable)` — the result is the callable's return value
- `Tasks.fromSupplier(description, supplier)` / `Tasks.fromRunnable(description, runnable)`
- `Tasks.fromValue(description, value)` — a constant
- `Tasks.fromClass(description, callableClass)` — a new instance is constructed on each execution, with full injection against the scope
- `Tasks.noop(description)` — does nothing
- `Tasks.transformResult(task, transformer)` — maps another task's result

### Task classes

A whole job can be one annotated class, compiled with `JobDefinition.fromTasks(...)`. Each `@Task` method is a task, executed in `order`; parameters are injected from the scope by type, and the return value is stored back under the method's `store` mode with a name derived from the returned type:

```java
public class ProvisioningTasks {

    @Task(order = 1)
    public ClusterSpec resolveCluster(Project project) { ... }   // stored as "clusterSpec"

    @Task(order = 2, store = StoreType.STATE)
    public TopicPlan planTopics(ClusterSpec cluster) { ... }     // durable decision

}

JobDefinition job = JobDefinition.fromTasks(ProvisioningTasks.class)
                                 .name("provision-kafka").version("1");
```

The class is instantiated once per run with constructor arguments resolved against the application context — it is never a Spring bean itself. Compilation fails fast on duplicate orders and on a task consuming a type that only a later task produces.

## The job scope

`JobContext` is the scope tasks share. Values stored by earlier tasks are available to later ones: beans by type through `@Autowired` injection or `getBean(Class)`, named values through `@Value("${name}")` or `getProperty(String)`. Lookups fall through parent scopes down to the application's own beans and configuration, so a task can inject platform services and job-produced values through the same mechanism.

## Storing results

How a value behaves on resume and whether watchers of the run may see it are independent choices, declared together on an immutable `Store`:

```java
.task(task)                                // keep nothing
.task(task.store(Store.none().wire()))     // keep nothing, publish to watchers
.task(task.store(Store.result("widget")))  // scope value, re-derived on resume
.task(task.store(Store.result("widget").wire()))
.task(task.store(Store.state("decision"))) // durable, replayed on resume
.task(task.store(Store.state("decision").wire()))
```

The `StoreType` axis answers *what survives a resume*:

- **NONE** — the value is discarded. On resume a completed task is skipped.
- **RESULT** — the value is stored in the scope but not persisted. On resume the task re-executes to regenerate it — or its declared reload task runs instead: `Store.result("workload").reload(reloadTask)` pairs a task that creates external state with the task that reloads it from its source of truth, so the creation is never repeated.
- **STATE** — the value is stored in the scope and serialized into the run's `TaskRecord`. On resume it is replayed from the record without executing. The value must survive a JSON round trip: a plain class or record with concrete field types. Generic values such as `List`, `Map`, and `Optional` are rejected at completion, because type erasure would make the record unrestorable.

The `wire()` axis answers *who may see it*: a wired value is serialized as JSON onto the run's `TaskCompletedEvent` and kept on the task's record as its `wireValue`, so watchers — including remote ones, which never receive live objects — can read it while the run executes and after it has finished. The `StoreType` decides what a resume replays; `wire()` decides what watchers see. Durable state stays private unless it opts in — the `stateValue` a resume replays never leaves the server — a result store can publish without being durable, and `Store.none().wire()` publishes a value that exists only for observers. Wire values only have to serialize, never deserialize, so the `STATE` restrictions on generics do not apply to them.

Use `STATE` for decisions and allocations the rest of the run depends on; use `RESULT` for lookups whose source of truth can answer again; add `wire()` for a result the run's remote watchers consume as data. What a console shows for a task is its view, declared separately (see [Presenting a task](#presenting-a-task)).

## Dynamic tasks

Structure can be decided at runtime: a task may return another `Task`, or a whole `JobDefinition`, instead of a value. Only work the task returns directly is dynamic; a `Task` or `JobDefinition` an asynchronous result completes with is a value, stored as any other. The returned work is discovered, reported to watchers as a `TasksDiscoveredEvent` flagged `dynamic` and carrying the producing task's path, and executed in place under that path. A dynamic `Task` that declares no `Store` of its own keeps its value as the producing task's `Store` declares; one that declares its own keeps it that way.

## Asynchronous results and Vert.x

A task may return its value directly, or asynchronously as a `CompletionStage`, a Vert.x `Future`, or a `Publisher` (whose last emission is the value) — the framework awaits it before storing.

Prefer the Vert.x `Future`: it is the platform's async type, and every platform repository and service already returns one. Return a `CompletionStage` only when a library offers nothing else — the Elasticsearch and Azure clients, for instance.

Every run executes on its own Vert.x virtual-thread context, and each parallel child gets its own. Inside a task, `Vertx.currentContext()` resolves, context-locals such as the platform `SecurityContext` participant work, blocking is permitted, and Vert.x futures can be awaited in place:

```java
String answer = vertx.timer(20).map(v -> "ticked").await();   // parks the virtual thread
```

**Never block on a future with CompletableFuture.get() or join() inside a task body.** Return the asynchronous value and let the framework await it, or await a Vert.x future in place with `.await()`. Both of those suspend the run's context so its queued work keeps flowing; `get()` and `join()` park the thread while it still holds the context, which stalls everything queued behind the task:

```java
@Task(order = 2)
public DeployTarget load(DeployTargetRepository repository, Project project) {
    return repository.findById(project.getId())
                     .toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().join();   // deadlocks the run
}

@Task(order = 2)
public Future<DeployTarget> load(DeployTargetRepository repository, Project project) {
    return repository.findById(project.getId());                          // the framework awaits it
}

@Task(order = 2)
public DeployTarget load(DeployTargetRepository repository, Project project) {
    return repository.findById(project.getId()).await();                  // or await it in place
}
```

How bad the stall is depends on where the future came from. A future bound to the run's context — anything a platform repository or service hands back — delivers its completion *through* that context, so `get()` waits on a completion queued behind itself and the run hangs permanently. A raw library future completes on its own thread, so the task does eventually proceed, but everything queued on the run's context — record writes, event delivery — waits until it does.

## Running and watching

`JobService` executes definitions:

```java
JobRunHandle handle = jobService.run(job, JobOwner.ofApplication(orgId, appId, projectId));
```

`JobOwner` records which tier the run executes on behalf of — `system()`, `ofOrganization(...)`, or `ofApplication(...)` — and, for an organization or application owner, the project the run served, so runs can be filtered by owner down to one project.

The handle pairs the persistent run's id with the run's event stream. **Execution is lazy**: nothing runs until the first subscriber attaches to `handle.getEvents()`, the job executes exactly once no matter how many subscribers attach, and every subscriber replays the full event history from the beginning. `handle.completion()` returns a future for the terminal outcome (subscribing, and so starting the run, if nothing else has), and `handle.cancel()` aborts the run, recording it as `CANCELLED`. Cancellation interrupts the run's thread, so a task blocked in an interruptible call is cancelled too, whatever exception the interrupted call throws.

The stream emits the sealed `JobRunEvent` family, each carrying the task's `taskPath` — its `/`-separated position in the run's task tree:

- **TasksDiscoveredEvent** — the task tree, at the start of the run and again as dynamic tasks appear; its `dynamic` flag says which, so watchers can mark the producing task the moment it reveals a subtree
- **TaskStartedEvent** — a task began executing, carrying the view it declares for its start
- **TaskProgressEvent** — a running task reported progress, a percentage and a message, or replaced its view, including the result view a task reports just before it completes
- **TaskCompletedEvent** — a task finished, carrying what it stored: the live value for in-process subscribers, and the JSON `wireValue` for wired stores
- **TaskFailedEvent** — a task terminated with a failure

The stream completes when the run does, and errors with the run's failure.

A run's live stream exists only in the process executing it. The run records the executing
node's id as `JobRun.nodeId`, so remote watchers route their watch request to that node - in a
cluster, any node can serve the persisted runs and records, while the live stream comes from
the one node named on the run.

## Presenting a task

A task declares how a console shows it. Its icon is the name of any [Lucide](https://lucide.dev/icons) icon, in Lucide's kebab-case form such as `folder-git-2`, set with `icon(...)` on the task, or `@Task(icon = ...)` on a task method:

```java
.task(Tasks.fromCallable("Sync project source", syncSource)
           .icon("folder-git-2"))
```

The icon is a fact of the definition, recorded on the task's `TaskRecord` from discovery, so a watcher shows it before the task runs. The console loads each icon's code the first time a task shows it; a name that is not a Lucide icon shows the console's default icon.

A task's detail pane shows a `TaskView`: the key of the component that renders it, and the data that component renders. A view is built through a `TaskViewKind`, which binds the key to the data's type, so a view of one kind cannot be built with another kind's data. Each domain module keeps the kinds its consoles render in one constants class:

```java
public static final TaskViewKind<WorkloadLog> WORKLOAD_LOG = new TaskViewKind<>("workloadLog");
```

A task declares the views it shows, and the latest one it produced is its current view:

```java
.task(Tasks.fromCallable("Sync project source", syncSource)
           .icon("folder-git-2")
           .startView(DeployTarget.class, target -> WORKLOAD_LOG.of(new WorkloadLog(target.syncWorkloadId()))))
.task(Tasks.fromCallable("Resolve artifacts", resolveArtifacts)
           .store(Store.state(ARTIFACTS))
           .resultView(PROJECT_ARTIFACTS::of))
```

- **startView(Source.class, source -> …)** — shown from the moment the task starts, for following what the task does while it runs. Just before the task executes, the value of the source type is looked up in the job scope the way `@Autowired` looks it up, so the data a live view needs must be in the scope when the task starts. A value the scope does not hold fails the task. The class names the source because Java erases a lambda's parameter type.
- **resultView(Result result -> …)**, or **resultView(Source.class, (Result result, Source source) -> …)** — shown once the task completes with a value, built from it: the value it returns, or the value a returned `Future`, `CompletionStage` or `Publisher` completes with. The producer names the result's type — as a method reference does, or as a lambda's declared parameter type — since the task's own type parameter is the future's; a result of another type fails the task. The view is reported as the task's last view, as `TaskReporter.view` reports one, and the task then completes with its result unchanged.
- **TaskReporter.view(view)** — replaces the view while the task runs, from inside the task body; see [Reporting progress](#reporting-progress).

A view reaches watchers on the task's own events — `TaskStartedEvent.view` and `TaskProgressEvent.view` — and the task's `TaskRecord` keeps the latest one in `view`, written whenever it changes, so a finished run, or one whose node left mid-task, shows what the task last showed. A failed task keeps the view it showed when it failed. A view's data is serialized as JSON when the view is produced, and reaches every watcher of the run, so it must never carry secrets. A producer that throws, or data that does not serialize, fails the task.

## Reporting progress

Each task is given a `TaskReporter` of its own in the scope it executes in, so a running task injects it like any other dependency and reports as it works — its progress, and, when what it shows changes, a new view:

```java
@Task(order = 1)
public void pullImage(TaskReporter reporter) {
    reporter.progress(30, "downloading layers");
    reporter.progress(80, "extracting");
}
```

Each report reaches watchers as a `TaskProgressEvent` attributed to the reporting task; a report that only replaces the view carries no percentage. A reporter accepts reports while its task is in flight — until the task's result has been awaited — from the task body and from callbacks dispatched on the run's Vert.x context, so a report made from a callback of the task's own `Future` belongs to the task, and one made after the task completed, or from a thread the task spawned itself, is dropped. A tasks class, one instance serving all its task methods, takes the reporter as a method parameter, as above; a `TaskReporter` field or constructor parameter on it fails `JobDefinition.fromTasks`. Progress is stream-only — it is not persisted with the run's records; a view is. Run-level progress needs no reports at all: watchers compute it from the discovered task tree and the completion events.

## Resuming a run

A `FAILED` or `CANCELLED` run can be resumed with a definition whose `name` and `version` match the recorded run:

```java
JobRunHandle resumed = jobService.resume(originalRunId, buildJob());
```

The resumed run is a new run — with its own id and records, linked to the original through `resumedFrom` and owned by whoever owned the original. Tasks the original run completed are handled by their `StoreType` as described above: skipped, re-run or reloaded, or replayed. A replayed `STATE` task builds its declared views from the scope and the replayed value; a skipped task, or a replayed one that declares no view, keeps the view the original run's record left it showing. A task that produced dynamic tasks re-executes so the dynamic structure is regenerated; the regenerated tasks then consult the original run's records at their own paths.

## Run records

Every run persists a `JobRun` — name, version, owner, status, timestamps, error, `resumedFrom`, and the `nodeId` of the executing node — and one `TaskRecord` per task: its `taskPath`, description, icon, status, timestamps, `storeType` and `storedName` (recorded from discovery when the definition names the store, so a watcher can tell the tasks apart before they complete), the serialized `STATE` value in `stateValue`, the wired value in `wireValue`, the latest view in `view`, and the failure message when it failed. The records are the run's durable history: what a dashboard renders after the event stream is gone, and what a resume replays from.

The ledger is written ahead of execution. Each transition is acknowledged by the store before the run moves past it: the `JobRun` and the `PENDING` records of the task tree before the first task starts, a task's `RUNNING` record before its body executes, its `COMPLETED` or `FAILED` record before the next task starts, and the terminal records before the event stream terminates — so a subscriber that sees the stream end can read the final ledger immediately. A node that goes down mid-run therefore leaves a `RUNNING` run whose records name exactly the task that was in flight, rather than losing the run. Every node watches the cluster membership, and a run still `RUNNING` on a node that is no longer a member is marked with the condition `SERVER_NODE_LEFT` on its `state.conditions`, since no node will report its end; the deployment that made the run, named in `state.parent`, is told, and its worker runs the deployment again. A run's terminal status is written in place, leaving that state as it is, and entered in the `kinotic_watch_event` ledger.

## Watching a run remotely

`JobService.watchRun(jobRunId)` attaches to a run executing in this process, replaying it from the start; it returns an empty stream for a run that has finished or never started, and subscribing never starts one. `JobMonitoringService` publishes that stream, and the records behind it, to remote callers in the management-api zone. Each node publishes its own instance, scoped by its node id: the finders are `@ScopeOptional`, so any instance answers an unscoped call, while `watch` must be invoked with the scope recorded on `JobRun.nodeId` — the node whose process holds the live stream:

```java
@Publish
public interface JobMonitoringService {

    @Scope
    String nodeId();

    @ScopeOptional
    Future<Page<JobRun>> findJobRuns(JobRunFilter filter, Pageable pageable);

    @ScopeOptional
    Future<JobRun> findJobRun(String jobRunId);

    @ScopeOptional
    Future<Page<TaskRecord>> findTasks(String jobRunId, Pageable pageable);

    Flux<JobRunEvent> watch(String jobRunId);

}
```

Every call is authorized against the run's recorded owner: an organization or application participant sees only the runs its organization owns, a system participant sees every run. `findJobRuns` narrows the runs on the server by the `JobRunFilter`'s organization, application, project, status and `startedSince`, a field left null matching every run, and its page carries the exact total the filter matches. An organization or application participant's runs are always narrowed to its own organization or application, and a filter naming another one fails. Events cross the wire as JSON carrying a `type` discriminator, and a `TaskCompletedEvent` arrives carrying only its `wireValue` — the live `storedValue` never leaves the executing process:

```json
{
  "type": "taskCompleted",
  "taskPath": "0/3",
  "storeType": "STATE",
  "storedName": "runtimeWorkloadId",
  "wireValue": "wl-8f21"
}
```

A run that is no longer live is rendered from `findJobRun` and `findTasks` alone, so a watcher that reaches a finished run sees the same history the stream would have delivered. The records `findTasks` returns carry a task's value only as its `wireValue`; their `stateValue` and `stateValueType` are cleared, so durable state a task did not wire stays on the server.

## System jobs

A system job is a grind job system users start on demand. Each is a Spring bean implementing `SystemJob`, whose one method builds a fresh, named and versioned definition for each run; its name identifies the job and is recorded on every run, so it must be unique among the system jobs:

```java
@Component
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class WorkloadRetentionJob implements SystemJob {

    private final Ignite ignite;

    @Override
    public JobDefinition createJobDefinition() {
        return JobDefinition.create("Deletes the records and logs of workload runs that ended more than 30 days ago")
                            .name("workload-retention-sweep").version("1")
                            .task(Tasks.fromCallable("Delete expired workloads", () -> {
                                WorkloadCleanupService.proxy(ignite).sweep();
                                return null;
                            }));
    }
}
```

The retention sweep runs on the cluster singleton that runs the hourly sweep, which runs one sweep at a time: a run started while a sweep is in progress joins it and completes when it ends.

`SystemJobService`, published in the system zone, lists them and starts them:

```java
@Publish
public interface SystemJobService {

    Future<List<SystemJobDescriptor>> findSystemJobs();

    Future<JobRun> startSystemJob(String name);

}
```

`findSystemJobs` describes each job by its definition's `name`, `version` and `description`, ordered by name; each job's definition is built once when the server starts to read them, and two jobs with one name fail the start. `startSystemJob` runs the named job on behalf of the system (`JobOwner.system()`) on the node that received the call, and completes with the `JobRun` once the run and its task ledger are recorded; it fails for a name no job has. From then on the run is an ordinary job run: listed, read and watched through `JobMonitoringService`.

The system console's **Jobs** page starts them: **Run system job** opens a drawer listing the jobs, and running one opens the new run's page. The page lists every run, the system jobs' runs among them, each marked as the system's. A run's page shows the run as the deployment pages do — its top-level tasks as a pipeline and its whole task tree, including every task a task generated as the run went.

### Workload logs

A step that runs a system workload shows the workload's console log on its row, the way a deployment's steps do: open while the step runs, following new lines once **Follow** is pressed, and readable afterwards from the run's history. The step declares the log as its start view, built from the scope value that holds the workload's id, which must therefore be in the job scope when the step starts (see [Presenting a task](#presenting-a-task)):

```java
.task(Tasks.fromCallable("Run the check's VM", runWorkload)
           .startView(CheckTarget.class, target -> TaskViews.WORKLOAD_LOG.of(new WorkloadLog(target.workloadId()))))
```

The log is read in the organization that owns the run: for a system job, the system's own log tenant, `kinotic-system`.

Kinotic ships one system job:

<table>

  <tr>
    <th>
      Name
    </th>

      What it does
    </th>
  </tr>
</thead>

<tbody>
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        workload-retention-sweep
      </code>
    </td>
    
    <td>
      Runs the <a href="https://kinotic.ai/platform/configuration#workload-retention">

      </a>

    </td>
  </tr>

# Project Publishing Design

> How a project's microservices and UIs are deployed, stored, and served, and how far the build has come.

## Overview

This page is the design record for publishing a project's artifacts: every microservice
under `packages/microservices` runs in a VM of its own, and every UI under `packages/ui`
is built by the deployment, uploaded to organization-owned Azure Blob storage, and served
on its own hostname through the Cloudflare sites Worker. It describes the target shape, and the
[Built so far](#built-so-far) section at the end says which parts exist today. The
user-facing view of the same flow is [Push to Deploy](https://kinotic.ai/apps/deployment/push-to-deploy).

## Entities

```text
ProjectDeployment            one per project: checkout dir, sync and publish VMs, job run, status,
  │                          the artifacts the last sync found and the commit it found them in
  ├─ MicroserviceDeployment  one per microservice artifact: its VM, its machine identity, the
  │                          commit it was ensured for, status
  └─ UiDeployment            one per UI artifact: its hostname, live
                             commit, status
```

"Deployment" names standing deployed state, as `ProjectDeployment` already does. Both
children are plain `AbstractRepository` entities in management-api beside `Workload`, not
organization-scoped ones. Each child has a published service for the console with
`findAllForProject` and `remove`, and UIs also have `findAllForApplication`; removal is the
only path that destroys anything.

Module placement follows the two servers the platform is splitting into: a management server
running management-api alone, which the portal and every organization machine reach, and a
system server running management-api and system-api, which the system console reaches. So
the records, their repositories and every service the portal calls live in management-api;
everything that touches nodes, workloads or Azure lives in system-api; and the management
plane reaches the second only through `DeploymentOperationsProxy`, a `@Proxy` interface onto
the system zone's `DeploymentOperationsService` (`restartMicroservice`, `removeMicroservice`,
`removeUiSite`), each of which writes intent that the deployment's worker carries out. The
management services authorize a request against the caller's organization, then delegate; the
operations service trusts its callers. A user of an organization, or a service acting for one, that
commits to a project's repository gets a token with contents write access to that one repository,
from the repository host (a GitHub installation token, or a Gitea token of an account that may write
that repository alone), through the management zone's `ProjectRepoCredentialService.issueWriteToken(projectId)`,
which issues tokens only for the projects of the caller's organization.
`ProjectDeployment` keeps the sync identity and loses `runtimeWorkloadId` and
`runtimeMachineIdentityId`, which move to the per-microservice rows.

## Artifacts and their identity

The [artifacts](https://kinotic.ai/apps/application-structure/artifact-types) a commit contains are found
inside the sync VM, over the checkout, by TypeScript in the workload-runner: code that sits
in the Bun ecosystem and can later resolve packages the way the project's own tooling
(`bunup`) does. For now the rule is naive and reads no Bun or bunup configuration: a
microservice is a package directly under `packages/microservices` with entry
`package.json.main`, else `src/main.ts`; a UI is a package directly under `packages/ui` with
a `build` script that writes `dist/index.html`. The UI location is the one requirement that
stays hard-coded when the resolution improves.

An artifact's identity is the unscoped part of the `name` in its `package.json`
(`@acme/admin` is `admin`), a single zone label, and a UI's without `--`; a name breaking
either rule fails the deploy naming the package. The directory name never matters. The sync VM reports what it found
through `ProjectArtifactService.recordArtifacts`, authenticated as the project's sync
machine identity, as one `ProjectArtifacts`: the commit it was found in, the artifacts, and the
`dependencyHash` of the checkout (a SHA-256 of `bun.lock` and of the version of the tree the SBOM
reads from it). The server
records it on `ProjectDeployment` and applies the same name rule to what it is told.

        ProjectArtifactService.recordSbom

Placement: every VM of a project shares the node holding its checkout. A first deployment's
probe wants `SYNC_MEMORY_MB + microservices × RUNTIME_MEMORY_MB`, but the artifacts are only known
after the sync VM has run on the chosen node; how the probe accounts for the microservices is
decided with the runtime-workload phase. The runtime workload of
each service sets `KINOTIC_APP_ENTRY = <dir>/<entry>`; the supervisor is unchanged.
`ProjectDeployIdentityService.issueRuntimeCredentials` reads and writes the identity id on
the `MicroserviceDeployment` row; the sync identity stays on `ProjectDeployment`.

## Storage

Published UIs live in the platform's **sites account**, one per environment (`st<env>sites`,
created by terraform, hierarchical namespace on, anonymous access off, public network open
since the edge reads from addresses the storage firewall cannot name, every read signed by a
read-only SAS on the container that terraform mints and binds to the Worker as a secret), where every site is one directory of the `sites` container named by its hostname, which is
what the sites Worker derives from a request's host:

```text
sites/orders--admin.acme.kinotic.io/index.html          Cache-Control: no-cache; uploaded last: the atomic switch
sites/orders--admin.acme.kinotic.io/version.json        Cache-Control: no-cache; { "commitSha": "<sha>" }
sites/orders--admin.acme.kinotic.io/assets/…            Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable; names carry a content hash
sites/orders--admin.acme.kinotic.io/…                   Cache-Control: no-cache; the rest of dist, e.g. favicon.ico
```

The server never touches a site's files. `SiteStorageService` issues the credentials the
workloads act with, each a user delegation SAS scoped to the one site's directory (`sr=d`,
signed through the Data Lake SDK): an upload URL (create, write, list, delete) for the
publish workload, and a removal URL (list, delete) for the removal workload. `dist` is
uploaded as it is, so a build needs no base path; every blob carries metadata `commit=<sha>`,
and once the index has switched the publish workload deletes every blob of the site stamped
with a commit other than the current one, listing its own directory through the blob
endpoint. A removal deletes the directory through the account's Data Lake endpoint in one
request.

## Serving

Nothing at the edge changes when a UI is published. Terraform's `modules/cloudflare-sites`
gives an environment, once: the zone's settings and Total TLS, the proxied records for the
app server's hosts, and the sites Worker (`deployment/cloudflare/sites-worker/worker.js`)
bound to every host of the sites domain and to none of the apps-api hosts. The Worker reads
the site from the request's host, `<app>--<ui>.<org>.<sitesDomain>`, or the application's
site for a tenant's host, `<tenant>--<app>--<ui>.<org>`, and the file from the path:

```text
a path whose last segment has an extension   →  sites/<site>/<path>        the file
any other path                               →  sites/<site>/index.html    a route of the single-page application
<org>.<sitesDomain>                          →  302 <portal>/login/<org>
```

Assets under `assets/` carry a content hash and are cached at the edge for a year; the
index and `version.json` for a minute, so a publish needs no purge. The account's container is
private: the Worker signs every read with a read-only SAS on the container, which terraform
mints for two years and re-mints yearly, so a yearly apply renews it with a year to spare; the
browser only ever sees the response.

Per organization the edge needs two proxied records, `*.<org>.<sitesDomain>` for its sites and
`<org>.<sitesDomain>` for its own host (a wildcard never matches its own label), which the
platform creates through `OrganizationDnsRecordProvisioner` when the organization is created and before
its first publish, and which Total TLS issues the organization's certificates from.
That is the one thing between a sign-up and a served site, and it completes in minutes with
nothing else to propagate; per-site domains, certificates and routes could never make a new
UI available within minutes of a publish, and that is why they do not exist.
`HttpUiDeploymentProvisioner` only reports: a site
is `PROVISIONING` from its first publish until `https://<hostname>/version.json` answers with
the deployment's commit and `https://<hostname>/` answers with HTML (a file bypasses the spa
rule), then `READY`: the deployment's worker, `UiDeployOrchestrator`, checks every 30 seconds
until the site serves the published commit, recording what the site answered on the row
meanwhile, and the reconcile master's resync brings a site back under check after a server
restart.

The hostname is `{app}--{ui}.{org}` under the sites domain (`kinotic.io`), minted at first
publish, stored as `UiDeployment.id` and looked up by hostname: the UI's label within the
organization's own subdomain. No organization id, application id or UI name contains `--`, and
the organization id `xn` is reserved so no label starts with DNS's `xn--`, so a hostname names
exactly one UI of one application of one organization; a site addressed to one tenant of the
application puts the tenant first, `{tenant}--{app}--{ui}.{org}`, which the edge serves from the
application's site. The repository's create enforces uniqueness: a UI name another project of
the application already published fails the publish. The first label is at most 37 characters,
DNS's 63 less the room a tenant's name (at most 24) and the separator take in front of it,
else the publish fails naming the organization and application.

## Auth

A site, `<app>--<ui>.<org>.kinotic.io`, is same-site with its application's API host,
`<org>--<app>.apps-api.kinotic.io`, so the app server's session cookie flows, and the app server's
CORS pattern admits the sites domain. The app server's session cookie is named
`__Host-kinotic-app-session` (Secure and `Path=/` are already set), `SameSite=Lax` unless
`kinotic.apiGateway.sessionCookieSameSite` says otherwise, as a developer's profile does when
the sites and the API sit on unrelated domains. `kinotic.io` is never put on the Public Suffix
List: an entry would make every site cross-site with the API hosts, and the host-only cookie
and the origin-bound login are what keep one site from reaching another's login.

## Build and upload contracts

The sync step sets, per UI build, `VITE_KINOTIC_HOST`, `VITE_KINOTIC_PORT` and
`VITE_KINOTIC_USE_SSL`, split from `KINOTIC_UI_SERVER_URL`: the application's API host,
`HostLabelUtil.apiUrl(kinotic.domain.appApiBaseUrl)` (`https://<org>--<app>.<apps-api domain>`),
placed on the sync workload by the job factory. The address the workload itself dials is for
egress and not usable by a browser. They are the variables the platform's own consoles
connect with, and Vite exposes them to the page without configuration. A build that leaves no `dist/index.html` fails the deploy before the
sentinel. `artifacts.ts` in workload-runner is the one enumeration of the artifacts, shared
by the sync and publish entrypoints.

The publish workload is named `project-ui-publish-<projectId>`, with id
`DeployTarget.uiPublishWorkloadId` decided in `resolveTarget` like `syncWorkloadId`. It runs
the same image in the foreground with entrypoint `bun src/publish-ui.ts`, the checkout mounted
read-only at `/workspace`, env `KINOTIC_UI_COMMIT`, and the secret `KINOTIC_UI_UPLOAD_URLS`, a
JSON object of UI name to `<blob endpoint>/sites/<hostname>?<directory SAS, create+write, TTL the run>`. Its allowed hosts are the sites account's host only; it carries no Kinotic
credentials and no machine identity, and is destroyed by the orchestrator as its run ends, the
way every foreground workload is. Its exit check is the one `syncSource` uses, extracted to one
method with two consumers. `publish-ui.ts` uploads, per UI, everything in `dist` into the site's directory: the files under
`assets/` with the immutable header, the rest uncached, then `version.json`, then
`index.html`, each a `PUT` with `x-ms-blob-type: BlockBlob`, `x-ms-blob-cache-control`,
`x-ms-meta-commit`, and a `Content-Type` from `Bun.file().type`; small concurrency, one retry
on 5xx, non-zero exit on failure.

## Orphans and removal

An artifact missing from a deploy marks its deployment `ORPHANED`; it keeps running or serving
and nothing is deleted. An artifact that returns is adopted (status back to `DEPLOYED` or
`READY`), never re-provisioned. `MicroserviceDeploymentService.remove` destroys the VM,
removes the identity, and deletes the row. `UiDeploymentService.remove` runs a removal
workload (`remove-ui.ts`, on the node the project deploys to, holding nothing but a removal
URL for the site's directory) that deletes the directory, then deletes the row; a project
never deployed has no node and its site no files, and a removal that fails leaves the files
for a later publish of the same label to adopt. Both confirm in the console when the
deployment is not orphaned.

## Properties and dependencies

`kinotic.domain.publishedSites.domain`, the sites domain every server shares, and `useSsl` and
`port`, which with it make each site's URL; `kinotic.systemApi.uiDeployment.sitesStorageEndpoint`;
and `kinotic.systemApi.uiDeployment.siteStorage`, which names the sites account (`AZURE`), the
Azurite emulator of a developer's machine (`AZURITE`) or no storage (`DISABLED`). Nothing else is a property; an organization has no storage of its own,
and nothing is provisioned when one is created.

Managed artifacts, each a `*Version` in `gradle.properties` and one line in the conventions
`dependencyManagement` block: `com.azure:azure-storage-file-datalake`, which signs the
directory SAS, and `com.azure:azure-storage-blob`, which it builds on, pinned at the version it
is built against. `azure-identity` is already managed; no management-plane SDK is.

## Deferred

Not part of this design: customer domains, an Environment entity, customer file storage, and
push notification of publishes.

## Built so far

- **Artifact discovery.** The sync VM finds the commit's artifacts (`src/artifacts.ts` in the
workload-runner, the naive rule above) and reports them through
`ProjectArtifactService.recordArtifacts`, which records `artifacts`, the commit they were found
in included, on `ProjectDeployment`. The deploy job's third task, **Resolve
artifacts**, binds them into the run as a `ProjectArtifacts` (its `MicroserviceArtifact`s
and `UiArtifact`s) under the `artifacts` store name, and shows them as its completion view. The
job run page of the portal and of the system console lists what the commit contains on that
task's row, and the sync task's row expands into the build VM's log in both.
- **One VM per microservice.** `MicroserviceDeployment` rows, keyed `<projectId>:<name>` so
the store enforces one per microservice, record each microservice's workload, machine
identity, entry point and commit. The deploy job's fourth task, **Ensure runtime workloads**,
keeps running VMs, replaces ended ones and ones whose entry point moved, creates missing ones,
orphans vanished ones, records failures per row, and stores the rows under
`microserviceDeployments`. `ProjectDeployment` no longer carries a runtime workload or
identity; `findProjectMachines` lists the sync identity then one per microservice.
- **Microservices in the console.** `MicroserviceDeploymentService` (`findAllForProject`,
`restart`, `remove`), published from management-api and reaching the VM through
`DeploymentOperationsProxy`, and the portal's deployment page: a microservices table with logs, restart and remove, and the
machines labelled by the deployment that records them.
- **UIs built in the sync VM.** After the entity sync, `sync.ts` runs `bun run build` in
every UI artifact with `VITE_KINOTIC_HOST`, `VITE_KINOTIC_PORT` and `VITE_KINOTIC_USE_SSL`,
split from the `KINOTIC_UI_SERVER_URL` placed on the sync workload from
`HostLabelUtil.apiUrl(kinotic.domain.appApiBaseUrl)`, and fails the run naming a UI whose build leaves no
`dist/index.html`.
- **UI deployments and the storage credentials.** `UiDeployment` rows keyed by the site's
hostname label, `SiteStorageService` (`issueUploadUrl`, `issueRemovalUrl`) signing
directory-scoped SAS through the Data Lake SDK on the sites account, each site's directory
named by its hostname, and the `UiDeploymentProvisioner` contract with a local provisioner
that marks sites ready at once.
- **The publish task.** The deploy job's fifth task, **Publish UIs**, mints the hostname
`{app}--{ui}.{org}` under the sites domain for each UI published for the first time, then runs
`project-ui-publish-<projectId>` under `DeployTarget.uiPublishWorkloadId` with
`publish-ui.ts`, the checkout read-only, `KINOTIC_UI_COMMIT`, the secret
`KINOTIC_UI_UPLOAD_URLS` (one one-hour directory SAS per site, by UI name) and the sites
account's hosts as its only egress, then finalizes: waits for new sites to serve, adopts
returning ones and orphans vanished ones; the workload itself deletes the files of other
commits once the index has switched. With site storage `DISABLED`
(`kinotic.systemApi.uiDeployment.siteStorage`) nothing serves, so nothing is uploaded. The exit
check is shared with the sync task, and the previous publish workload is retired by the next
run's target resolution.
`SiteWorkloadFactory` builds the publish workload and the removal workload alike.
- **The project SBOM.** A project has one commit and one dependency hash, both on
`ProjectDeployment.artifacts`; `ProjectDeployment.sbomGenerated` says whether the project's
`ProjectDependencies` list those dependencies, and `recordArtifacts` clears it when a sync
reports another hash. The deploy job's sixth task, **Generate SBOM**, runs
`project-sbom-<projectId>` under `DeployTarget.sbomWorkloadId` only while the flag is clear:
`generate-sbom.ts` reads the dependency tree of the read-only checkout's `bun.lock`, resolving
each dependency the way bun loads it (for a package at key `a/b`, the first of `a/b/d`, `a/d`
and `d` the lockfile holds), and records it with `recordSbom` as the sync machine, whose
secret is reissued for it; the workload's only egress is the server, and the record is refused
unless its hash is the one the sync reported. The server stores the tree as one document per
project in `kinotic_project_dependencies`: `packages`, a keyword list of package URLs, so the
projects holding a package are one term query, and `direct`, `development`, `optional` and
`edges` as unindexed positions in it. The portal's SBOM page reads the tree through
`ProjectService.findDependencies` and builds the CycloneDX document it downloads in the
browser. A project's deletion deletes the tree with its deployment.
- **Sites on Cloudflare.** Terraform's `modules/cloudflare-sites` owns everything a site needs, once
per environment: the zone's settings and Total TLS, the app server's proxied hosts, and the
sites Worker that serves `sites/<hostname>/` from the sites account, which `modules/sites`
owns with the server identity's Storage Blob Data Contributor on it. An organization owns no
storage; its one provisioned thing is the record `*.<org>.<sitesDomain>`, which
`OrganizationDnsRecordProvisioner` creates at sign-up and before the first publish. `HttpUiDeploymentProvisioner` creates nothing: it answers
whether a published site serves its commit through `version.json` and its index through
the edge, and the deployment's worker keeps asking until it does, then reports `READY`.
- **UI deployments in the console.** `UiDeploymentService` (`findAllForProject`,
`findAllForApplication`, `remove`),
published from management-api and delegating to the system server through
`DeploymentOperationsProxy`: remove asks for the deployment's removal, and its worker takes the site down,
deletes the UI's prefix in storage and deletes the row. Deleting a project removes
its UI deployments the same way. `@kinotic-ai/management-api` exposes it as
`Kinotic.uiDeployments` with the `UiDeployment` model.
- **Sites in the console.** `UiDeployment.url` is minted with the
label, so the portal's deployment page lists each UI with a link to its site, the phase it
reports and the commit it serves, with removal. Each server's session cookie is `__Host-kinotic-<server>-session`,
named once in `ApiGatewayVertcleFactory` from the server's `ZonePartitioningService` and handed to the
gateway's session handler and to the `SessionBinding` that resolves each page's login from it.


# Sign-In Design

> How OIDC configurations, scoped logins and the one-user-per-scope model fit together, in seven figures.

## Overview

Seven pictures of how sign-up and sign-in fit together: who owns a provider configuration and where its secret lives, the configuration classes, how a configuration's kind decides which login offers it, the two routes a browser can take through the app server, the identity and participant classes, how one person is a separate user of each organization, and the doors on the management server. [Organization Management](https://kinotic.ai/platform/organization-management) walks the same flows endpoint by endpoint and [System Security](https://kinotic.ai/platform/system-security) states the rules they enforce; this page is the map.

## Two owners, two keys into one vault

A system user and an organization administrator each write their own kind of configuration. Only the system user's kind can name a secret in the vault. An organization's kind has no such field at all: its secret is handed to the service at save time and stored under the organization's own scope, so nothing an organization writes can reach a system secret.

<sign-in-flows-diagram figure="owners">



</sign-in-flows-diagram>

Each owner's kind reaches the vault by its own key. The red path is the point of the design: an organization's row has nowhere to write a system secret's name.

- `OidcConfiguration` is sealed: `ManagedOidcConfiguration` (`ORG_SIGNUP` for GitHub sign-up, `APP_SOCIAL` for Google and Microsoft) and `OwnedOidcConfiguration`, whose concrete kind is the scope it is offered at: `ORGANIZATION`, `APPLICATION`, `TENANT`. All are documents in one index, `kinotic_oidc_configuration`, read back by their `type`.
- An organization names its account at a provider, never a URL. The issuer is derived from the provider's template on every save, so the server only ever connects to the provider's own hosts. The organization's configurations are managed on the Authentication providers tab of its settings page, an application's and a tenant's on the application's settings page, or through `OwnedOidcConfigurationService`.
- Deleting an organization's configuration deletes its secret. A save without a secret keeps the one held; `deleteClientSecret` removes it, which makes the configuration a public client whose sign-in never reads the vault. A copy to another scope (`copy`) gets its own callback URL and its own copy of the secret.

## The configuration model

One sealed hierarchy. The abstract root carries what every provider needs; the two abstract branches carry what distinguishes the system's registrations from an organization's own; and each leaf adds only the ids that name the scope it is offered at. The leaf type is the `type` discriminator the index stores.

<sign-in-flows-diagram figure="model">



</sign-in-flows-diagram>

The leaf a configuration is saved as is its scope: a leaf with no scope id is the organization's own login, `applicationId` names an application's, `applicationId` plus `tenantId` a tenant's. An `ApplicationOidcConfiguration` whose `clientRegistrationType` is `MANAGED` is the only reference to a managed registration an organization ever holds, and it names it by provider kind alone.

- Only a managed registration can name a secret (`secretNameRef`) or set the explicit endpoint fields GitHub needs instead of discovery. An owned configuration derives its authority from `provider` and `providerAccount` on every save.
- The hierarchy is sealed on both levels, so every `switch` over a configuration's kind is exhaustive, and a new scope is a new leaf plus a new `OidcConfigurationType` constant.

## Which login offers a configuration

Nothing is embedded in an organization or an application, and there is no join row. An owned configuration is offered at exactly the scope its kind names; an organization that wants the same Okta tenant at its own login and at an application's copies the configuration into the application's scope. The system's GitHub registration is offered at every organization's login by right. The system's social registrations are never offered on their own: an application's configuration of their provider kind signs in through one when its `clientRegistrationType` is `MANAGED`, and is offered at the application's login like any other of its configurations. A tenant's login offers the tenant's configurations first, then everything the application's login offers.

<sign-in-flows-diagram figure="offering">



</sign-in-flows-diagram>

What reaches each login and why: an org sign-up registration by right, an owned configuration at the one scope its kind names, and a social registration through an application's `MANAGED` configuration only, never at the organization's own login.

- Every read and write of an owned configuration is held to the caller's organization, and a copy is refused for an application or tenant the organization does not have.
- A `createUserOnSignIn` flag on an application's or a tenant's configuration creates the identity its provider verifies as a user of that scope on the first sign-in: a user of the application, with a tenant of its own while the system manages the application's tenants, or a user of the tenant for a `TENANT` kind. Email and password is a provider of the same lists, a `PasswordConfiguration` of an organization's, an application's or a tenant's login, which takes a password only while one of its scope is enabled; an application whose tenants the system manages may let people sign up with it, with the configuration's own `createUserOnSignIn`, verified by an emailed link. `GET /api/auth/app/login/methods` tells a page whether its login takes a password, whether the password sign-up is open, and which of its providers sign people up. An organization's configuration refuses the flag: its members are added by administrators, and its provider then signs them in.

## Where the provider sends the browser back

An application's login page offers every method up front: the password form and a button per offered configuration. No endpoint takes an email before the user has chosen. An application's configuration then signs in through one of two registrations with the provider, and they differ in exactly one thing: where the provider returns the browser. The organization's own client (`OWN`) returns to the application's host. Kinotic's registration (`MANAGED`) is shared by every application and can only return to one place, so it returns to the app server's shared host, which finds the user and hands the sign-in to the application's host under a single-use code.

<sign-in-flows-diagram figure="paths">



</sign-in-flows-diagram>

Same start, same ending. Path B adds the shared host between the provider and the application's host, and nothing else. A sign-in from a tenant's site takes the same paths with the tenant stashed on the flow. Black arrows are the browser calling a host; green, the application's host answering; violet, the shared host; amber, the provider.

- The start is `POST /api/auth/app/login/oidc/start/:configId` on the application's host. It refuses a page that is not one of the application's UIs, a page that is a site of another tenant, and a configuration the login does not offer, then answers `{redirect}`.
- In path B the shared host runs the provider round-trip through the system registration on its own session, holding the application's configuration the flow started with. The application's host accepts the code once, only if it was staged for that very application and presented by the browser that started the sign-in, and then establishes the session exactly as path A does.
- Either callback finds the application's user through the binding of the application's configuration and the identifier the provider gives the person under every client (`sub`, or `<tid>/<oid>` for Microsoft), so a configuration switched between `MANAGED` and `OWN` finds the same users; an identity no user is bound to claims the pending user an administrator added to the scope under its email, and otherwise is created as a user where the configuration signs people up (`ApplicationSignUpService.findOrCreateOidcUser`); then the callback checks the user belongs to the login's scope: a tenant's login admits that tenant's users only. The code is random, dies on first use or after a minute, and carries only the user's id.
- The password form posts to `POST /api/auth/app/login` and answers 204 with the cookie, or a generic 401.

## The identity and participant model

Three kinds of identity share one sealed root, and a person is one of three kinds of user, each the user of one scope: a system user, an organization user and an application user. An organization user, an application user, a delegate and a machine are each a `ScopedParticipantIdentity`, which carries the scope it acts in: `organizationId` for an organization user, `organizationId` and `applicationId` for the others. A system user acts in the system scope and has neither. A user's sign-in methods are rows of their own that point back at the user. What a request runs as is a `Participant`: the identity acting in its scope.

<sign-in-flows-diagram figure="identity">



</sign-in-flows-diagram>

An identity row says who; a participant says who, acting where. Every identity carries its own scope, so `createParticipant(identity)` makes its participant, and `resolveParticipant(identityId, organizationId, applicationId)` admits it only in the scope it carries, a delegate only while its owner may act there, and a disabled identity nowhere.

- The index mappings follow the classes one to one: `kinotic_participant_identity` for the sealed root with its subclass fields, `kinotic_identity_credential` and `kinotic_oidc_binding`.
- `ParticipantIdentityType` {SYSTEM_USER, ORGANIZATION_USER, APPLICATION_USER, DELEGATE, MACHINE} is the discriminator the index stores for the root, as `OidcConfigurationType` is for configurations. A delegate and a machine authenticate as their type says; a user's methods are its credential and binding rows, and `AuthType` {PASSWORD, OIDC} names one of them on the Profile page.
- Each login authenticates the kind of user its scope holds, so one email may be a user of every scope, each with its own password: the system console finds system users, an organization's login organization users, an application's login that application's users.

## One user per organization

A person who uses the portal holds a separate organization user in each organization they belong to, unique by email within that organization, each with its own password, bindings and `enabled` flag. Every login is addressed to one organization and signs in that organization's user, and a session acts in that organization alone; using another is a sign-in at that organization's login.

<sign-in-flows-diagram figure="organization-user">



</sign-in-flows-diagram>

Two rows, one per organization: the methods that sign the user in, the user, and the organization it belongs to. One GitHub account is bound separately in each organization. Each login below reads one binding or credential, so nothing in the login path waits on an index refresh.

- Disabling or removing a member touches that organization's user alone. Removing a member deletes the user with its credential, bindings and delegates, and the person's users of other organizations stay as they are.
- A delegate (the CLI, an MCP host) is unique per owner and client, carries its owner's organization, and authenticates only while its owner may still act there.
- The system console signs in system users, a separate row for the same person with a password of its own.

## The doors on the management server

Organization users sign up and in on the management server. Every door produces or finds a user of one organization; none of them asks about an email before a method is chosen, and a signed-in organization user manages its own methods from the Profile page. An administrator adds a member from the Members page: the organization's user exists at once, pending, until an invitation or the organization's own provider claims it.

<sign-in-flows-diagram figure="doors">



</sign-in-flows-diagram>

Four doors on one host. A new organization user appears through the first three: founded with a new organization at sign-up, added by an administrator, or created by an invitation. The fourth is where a signed-in organization user adds a method; the only other ways a provider identity joins a user that already exists are an invitation or the organization's own provider claiming a pending member.


# Service Call Liveness

> How a call through a service proxy fails when the node serving it dies, instead of waiting forever — without a timeout anywhere.

## Overview

A [service proxy](https://kinotic.ai/apps/services/service-proxies) call travels over the OS bus to whichever node hosts the service — another server's node for a Java service, or a gateway socket for a TS service running on a [workload node](https://kinotic.ai/platform/architecture). If that node dies while the call is in flight, nothing would ever answer the caller. Kinotic handles this as a property of the platform rather than of each call: **no service call carries a timeout, and none needs one.** Instead, every hop that holds a pending request watches the *registration* of the callee that serves it, and fails the request the moment that registration is gone.

The reason to prefer this over a timeout is that a timeout encodes a guess about how long work takes, and no number is right for a service the platform does not own. Liveness observes whether the worker still exists. A legitimate ten-hour call is never cut short; a dead node fails its pending calls within seconds.

<callout type="info">

**Implementation status.** The terminal reply marker every part of this design reads is in place, and so are the acknowledgement that names the node, the cluster membership signal a pinned lease checks it against, and the request liveness watcher Java callers and the MCP invoker take their leases through, together with the graceful stop on the callee side, and the gateway holds a lease for every request it forwards for a TS client, answers the client with the typed error when the serving node leaves, and answers every requester of a TS service instance whose connection closes mid-call. A connection that closes releases everything held for it on both ends, so no call outlives its connection. The wire contract and error types below are the ones callers see.

</callout>

## Registration is liveness

A service is reachable exactly while its address has an entry in the cluster's replicated subscription cache. That cache is maintained by the Vert.x cluster manager on Ignite, and Ignite removes a dead node's entries as part of its own failure detection. The platform already turns those updates into a push signal: the [callee side](https://kinotic.ai/apps/services/streaming) of a streaming call watches the *caller's* reply destination and cancels the stream when the caller disappears; for a TypeScript service the gateway holding its connection does the watching and delivers the cancel over the socket. Liveness for callers is the same signal, in the other direction.

<rpc-liveness-diagram view="overview">



</rpc-liveness-diagram>

Reading the diagram: every pending request is a **lease** pinned to the node whose acknowledgement took it, held at whichever hop has cluster visibility. A Java caller and the MCP invoker are in the cluster and take leases directly through the request liveness watcher. A TS client — the UI, or a TS service calling another service — is outside the cluster and cannot see registrations, so the **gateway** takes the leases on its behalf and answers the client with an error reply when one fails. The watcher holds one cluster membership subscription per node, however many requests are in flight, and it rides on the discovery events the cluster already delivers to every node; nothing new is replicated. The count of requests it holds is the `rpc.pending.requests` gauge.

The signal that ends a request is the same one every reply already carries: a terminal reply is marked `control: complete` on the event itself, so any hop can release its lease on that one event without knowing whether the method returned a value, nothing, or a stream.

## A call in flight when its node dies

The ack that confirms receipt of a request names the node whose consumer took it. That matters for any address with more than one registration: a service published on several nodes, several TS instances of one service, or the shared address a scoped service joins for its [`@ScopeOptional`](https://kinotic.ai/apps/reference/decorators) methods. A call to such an address lands on one instance, the address stays active as long as *any* instance lives, and the caller must know which one took its request.

<rpc-liveness-diagram view="failure">



</rpc-liveness-diagram>

A lease starts at the ack. Before it, Vert.x itself bounds the send: the request fails at once when nothing is registered, and after its delivery timeout when the ack never arrives — a bound on one network hop, not on the call, since the consumer acks before it dispatches. From the ack on, the lease is pinned to the node that answered and fails when that node leaves the cluster, even while other instances keep the address active, and even after that node has unregistered the address to drain before shutting down. A node that finishes a call before it leaves never fails it.

For a TS service the ack names the gateway holding the instance's subscription, which cannot tell two TS instances on the same gateway apart. The gateway can: it forwarded the invocation to one specific socket and sees the terminal reply come back through the same connection, so it tracks each outstanding invocation per socket and synthesizes the failure for all of them when that socket closes. STOMP heartbeats make a socket close deterministic even when a VM vanishes without closing it: the gateway offers and expects a 30 s heartbeat in both directions and closes a connection silent for two intervals, so this path is bounded by the heartbeat interval — ahead of Ignite's own detection window. The TS client offers and expects the same 30 s, so a gateway that vanishes without closing the socket is a connection loss on the client within two intervals as well, and the calls on it fail through the rule below.

What the caller receives, in every runtime:

<table>
<thead>
  <tr>
    <th>
      Exception
    </th>
    
    <th>
      Meaning
    </th>
    
    <th>
      The call…
    </th>
  </tr>
</thead>

<tbody>
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        RpcMissingServiceException
      </code>
    </td>
    
    <td>
      rejected at send, no registration for the address
    </td>
    
    <td>
      never executed
    </td>
  </tr>
  
  <tr>
    <td>
      <code>
        RpcServiceUnavailableException
      </code>
    </td>
    
    <td>
      the node that took the call left the cluster while it was in flight, its acknowledgement never arrived, or the service stopped while producing a stream
    </td>
    
    <td>
      may or may not have executed
    </td>
  </tr>
</tbody>
</table>

Callers of non-idempotent operations should treat the second as ambiguous and check before retrying. In TypeScript a failed call rejects with an `RpcError`, whose `exceptionName` and `exceptionClass` name the exception the server caught — for a service hosted in TypeScript, the class of the error it threw, whose name fills both — so a caller branches on `exceptionName === 'RpcServiceUnavailableException'` rather than on the message.

A service that stops, on a rolling update or any other graceful shutdown, stops accepting calls first, then answers every call it already has before its node leaves the cluster, so those calls complete normally and no lease fails. Streams it was producing cannot be finished; each one ends with `RpcServiceUnavailableException` at its subscriber the moment the service stops. The wait for the in-flight calls is bounded, so a call that never finishes cannot hold the shutdown.

## Reconnects and node rollovers

A call is bound to the connection it was made on. When that connection closes, for any reason, both ends let go at the same moment: the gateway unregisters the connection's reply consumer and releases its leases, so a server stream producing for it is cancelled through the reply-listener path and no reply is held anywhere, and the client fails every call it had in flight with `Connection lost`, streams included, the moment it observes the close. A reconnect starts clean. Nothing waits for a client to come back, so nothing can wait on the wrong node, and a node that dies takes no client's pending replies with it because it was holding none.

This is the deliberate choice over holding replies for a returning client. The STOMP port sits behind a load balancer with no session affinity, so a reconnect lands on any gateway node; buffering replies on the node that lost the connection would only pay off with a cross-node handoff, and a handoff still loses the buffer when that node dies. Retrying a call is the cheaper contract. For a caller that needs a message to survive its connection, that is a delivery guarantee, and it belongs in a queue behind the API with acknowledgement and redelivery, not in a reply buffer on a gateway.

## What this does not cover

A callee that is alive and registered but wedged — deadlocked, or looping — produces no liveness signal, and no mechanism short of a deadline could catch it. That is a misbehaving service rather than a failed node, and the watcher exposes the count of pending requests per node so that it becomes visible in [observability](https://kinotic.ai/platform/observability) as a count that climbs on a healthy node. If it ever needs bounding, a deadline declared by the service on its own contract composes with everything above; a timeout guessed by the caller does not.


# Supply Chain Security

> How Kinotic inventories, scans and gates the container images it publishes, and where the evidence for each control is kept.

## Overview

Every Kinotic service image is inventoried and scanned for known vulnerabilities before it is published. An image with a Critical vulnerability that has a published fix is never promoted to Docker Hub. Every control on this page runs automatically in the `Build and Publish` workflow (`.github/workflows/gradle-build.yml`), and each one leaves evidence in GitHub.
